#6680. The 28 Best Hostess Gifts Guaranteed to Secure You an Invite Back

If one of life’s simple pleasures is going to a friend’s house for a home-cooked meal, one of life’s great conundrums is figuring out the art of the host gift. If you bring a dessert, should you poll for food allergies ahead of time? Does anyone really need more scented candles? And what about the much-maligned bottle of wine?

I host a pasta dinner nearly every Monday, and for what it’s worth, I’m always happy when someone shows up with a wine we can pour with the meal. I’ve had people bring a really great wheel of brie and I’ve had people bring a plant stand for a kumquat tree in my kitchen whose sad drooping they’d noticed at dinner the week before. Recently, one friend appeared with a calendar of Italian priests. Am I Catholic? No. Is it a newly prized possession, hanging prominently on the wall by the bread basket (it felt apropos)? Of course. The best hostess gifts don’t adhere to any strict guidelines; they’re the ones that show your friends know you, and put a little thought into what to get you when—to quote the cliché—they really shouldn’t have.

Whether your calendar is filling up with holiday parties or you’ve befriended someone with a weekend home Upstate, this time of year is rife with occasions that call for these sort of trinkets. And since there’s no such thing as a one-size-fits-all option, it’s worth taking a little time to pinpoint a present with a little personality.

The below is an assortment of the very best hostess gift ideas. If you’re looking for something small and sure to please, an edible treat is a safe bet; if you’re looking for a larger gift, say, for a birthday or a holiday, for your friend who loves to entertain, this is for you too. Herewith, a curated gift selection by type of host—and plenty of pieces you might want to earmark for yourself while you’re at it.

You love them not because they can whip up a multi-course meal on demand, but because they know all the best spots to order a multi-course meal on demand. Dress up pizza from the place around the corner with an infused oil, or zhuzh up the dessert course with resin ice cream spoons.

Bagged leftovers aren’t boring—they’ve just been missing a delightful fish clip to keep them secure.

Brightland’s finishing oil comes infused with herbs and spices like jalapeño, garlic, and basil to turn any dollar slice gourmet.

Dress up take-out boxes with the help of printed napkins. These, inspired by Byzantine mosaics, will make pretty much anything look fancy.

The host with the most—but the least amount of space—has mastered the art of the tiny apartment dinner party. Gift them something useful that won’t eat away at valuable cupboard space: a Japanese-inspired bento bag that moonlights as a makeshift bread basket and folds up when guests leave, for example, or a tiny espresso maker for after-dinner coffees.

This trio of miniature clay pots forms the base of a well-equipped windowsill herb garden.

Inspired by Japanese furoshiki, this linen bread basket folds up flat when not in use.

The original 1960s design needs no improvement: Here’s a compact, cheery solution to bulky coffee machines.

#6679. 21 Easy Weeknight Dinners for November

As daylight dwindles and the November chill settles in, dinner calls for something cozy. Think chicken thighs nestled into caramelized onions, pasta slicked with brown butter, and hearty soups that practically demand a hunk of crusty bread. It’s time to lean into comfort food.

Greek yogurt tenderizes the chicken quickly, but the real weeknight win is the broiler: just 15 minutes under high heat, and you’ve got dinner.

Juicy chicken meatballs and crisp-tender sesame green beans roast on opposite sides of the same sheet pan, streamlining both dinner prep and cleanup.

This speedy stir-fry recipe brings together thin strips of boneless pork shoulder and crisp-tender bok choy for a satisfying, weeknight-ready dinner.

Savory ground beef, fluffy scrambled eggs, and crisp vegetables turn a bowl of steamed rice into a satisfying Japanese dinner that’s ready in 35 minutes.

Buttery, garlicky shrimp scampi meets pasta in this weeknight-friendly dinner. A splash of white wine and a pinch of red pepper flakes make the sauce sing.

Four ingredients are all you need for these grown-up buttered noodles. Toasted almonds and parsley are totally optional, but add welcome texture and zing.

Pumpkin purée adds richness, body, and a gentle orange hue to this speedy ground beef chili, letting the flavors of the spices and aromatics shine.

When dinner needs to get on the table pronto, a tuna melt is hard to beat: pantry-friendly, cheesy, and comforting.

This fiery soup has a shockingly trim ingredient list: curry paste (we like Maesri), a can of pumpkin purée, and coconut milk. Perfect for busy November weeknights.

#6677. 16 Best Automatic Watches for Men 2026, According to GQ Watch Nerds

A budding “watch guy” most likely starts off their collection with an assortment of quartz tickers (and let’s be clear, there’s nothing wrong with that). But as your interest in watches grows, it’s only natural for you to want something on your wrist you can brag about, which inevitably pushes you towards automatic watches.

Inside the case of an automatic watch is a weighted rotor that spins as you move your arm, a few little flicks of your wrist throughout the day keeps the internal mechanisms running long enough to keep that minute hand tick-tick-ticking across the dial.

But automatic watches also have a reputation for being finicky or costly. And while that can be true, the beauty of watches is the wide price scale in which the industry operates. From stunners for less than $250 to ones you’d have to mortgage your house (and maybe your parents’ house) to buy, here are the top automatic watches on the market today for any budget.

While not impossible to find a great watch at the $250-mark, you are going to be limited. Given the many internal pieces and complicated mechanisms needed to build an automatic watch, many brands have to charge a bit more for a quality automatic. Even so, brands like Orient and Seiko lead the way on well-made (and well-designed) options.

Orient’s range of inexpensive watches punch well above their weight-class and the Symphony III is no different. With its classic, clean design and movement that promises 40 hours of power reserve, this is a watch that’s made to be a daily driver without breaking the bank.

Timex’s Waterbury is a staple in their line-up and the extremely stylish Metrograph has an Art Deco-style case and dial that’s pared-down enough to keep things simple, but without looking boring.

The Seiko 5 is something of a cult favorite for the Japanese brand – and for good reason. It’s a perfect daily driver and a budget-friendly alternative to the Rolex Datejust. Best of all, it clocks in at just 37mm, which is the perfect case size for nearly any wrist.

As ever, Timex provides maximum bang for minimum buck with this classic "Pepsi" bezel diver.

At $500, the doorway starts to open up a bit more – but only a creak. The usual suspects like Timex and Casio, are populating this price point, Bulova and Sternglas are great alternatives who will give you a little more street cred among collectors.

Undoubtedly one of the best looking watches in the sub-$500 category, the Timex Marlin in this particular shade of green strikes the perfect balance between classic and modern.

Heavily influenced by motorsports, the Edifice is a bit of a departure from the digital, retro-charm of many mainstays for Casio. The integrated bracelet keeps it sporty, while the patterned dial makes it a little more interesting than other options on the market.

At 45mm, 200-meter of water resistance, and 42-hours of power reserve, the Bulova Marine Star ticks all the boxes for a great dive watch at a reasonable price – the two-toned bezel is just a nice bonus.

This fan favorite hits the bullseye of the style-quality-price nexus, and looks especially fetching with a bright yellow dial.

A thousand bucks is a perfectly reasonable budget to have when you want to upgrade your watch game without completely breaking the bank. Here, I’d recommend looking at smaller, or more indie brands to find some interesting designs not seen by more household names.

You’d be forgiven for not knowing their name, but Kuoe is starting to gain traction in the U.S.. The Japanese-based watchmaker produces high-quality, well-designed pieces that harken to a more classic watch style. The OLD SMITH is based on the military field watch, but with a slightly more refined design language.

A reborn grail from the Studio 54 era, with a vintage-correct 35mm case.

UNIMATIC uses the basic field watch as the springboard for their Modello Due, which strips it back to its barebones to make something a bit bolder, a bit more modern, and eye-catching.

Paulin is a Glasgow-based microbrand that’s known for colorful, unique, and whimsical watches, often playing with color to make their designs all the more interesting.

Needless to say, if money isn’t an issue, the sky’s the limit. Not all watches are created equal and buying just for the name recognition alone doesn’t always make for the best watch for the money. Instead, look for a price point that’s commensurate with the movement, design, and materials used, and you’ll never regret the decision to spend the big bucks.

Taken from a 1924 archival design, the Brunswick’s cushion case, clean lines, and mother-of-pearl dial may all feel a bit “precious”, shall we say; but this is a workhorse watch that’s destined to be a daily driver for anyone who is looking for a little eye-candy on the wrist.

The IWC Ingenieur is a masterfully made ceramic watch (and matching ceramic bracelet) that will no doubt get you a few compliments every time you wear it to the office.

Not many watches can be mistaken for a Bell & Ross watch with its larger proportions and signature square case shape. The BR-05, the brand’s most popular model, is a sportier, slightly bolder answer to Cartier’s Santos.

It’s hard to narrow down one Grand Seiko to choose, but the White Birch is subtle and versatile enough to dress up or use as your daily driver. Most impressive about this particular model is the Caliber 9SA5 movement, which promises a whopping 80-hours of power when fully wound – nearly twice that of many others on the market.

Mechanical watch movements fall into two basic categories: hand-wound and automatic. Before the invention of automatic wristwatches in the 1920s (and long before the invention of battery-powered quartz movements in the 1960s) all watches were hand-wound. That meant you needed to manually wind up your watch every day to keep it running. An automatic watch (also called a self-winding watch) doesn’t require this because it winds automatically with the movement of your body as you wear it.

Most automatic watches wind themselves via a weighted rotor, which you’ll be able to see if your watch has a see-through case back (it’s the half moon-shaped piece right on top). When you wear the watch and move around, the rotor winds a spring, which turns the hands, date wheel and everything else that moves on a watch.

To keep your watch from stopping when you’re sitting still (or when you take it off at night) automatic movements also store excess energy and slowly release it over hours or days while the rotor is stationary. This is called a “power reserve,” and it typically ranges from 40 to 80 hours, with some going as high as a week or more. They’re useful if you don’t wear a watch every day, and don’t want to have to reset the date and time every time you put it on—particularly with annual or perpetual calendar models that can be complicated to set.

It’s not a downside, per se, but they do require some upkeep. Unlike a quartz watch that requires nothing more than a new battery every few years, a mechanical watch is a finely-tuned machine consisting of many tiny, precisely calibrated parts. Watchmakers have made huge advances in shock-and waterproofing over the years, but there’s still only so much abuse a mechanical movement can take. And that’s the thing: repairs to automatic watches can be expensive.

If you stick to the manufacturer’s recommended service schedule (it’ll need an overhaul and lube every 4 to 10 years, depending on the brand and model) and don’t make a habit of wearing it in the sauna, you’ll probably be fine. Whether it’s a $200 Amazon special or a $200,000 grand complication, automatic watches are designed to be worn, so the best way to take care of your watch is to wear it as much as possible.

Style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

We lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally new to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

Whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you. (Read more about GQ's testing process here.)

#6676. How Her Love of Vintage Changed Writer Keli Goff’s Life

Her collection, which has given new life to some of the great Black designers, is now a museum show.

When Keli Goff began purchasing vintage, it was a way to put together stylish looks for her new job within her budget. But over the years, as her interest grew, collecting became a way of connecting to the stories of Black designers unrecognized during their lifetimes. Goff, a writer who has been on the staff of shows including Being Mary Jane and And Just Like That, now owns work from major fashion figures like Patrick Kelly, Isaia Rankin, Stephen Burrows, and Ann Lowe, together making up one of the biggest private collections of work by Black designers. This month, the Houston Museum of African American Culture presents “Collecting in Color: Highlights from the Keli Goff Collection,” which was curated by John Guess and Danielle Finnerman. It’s the first major exhibition focused on her collection, and some of the pieces will be donated to the Bard Graduate Center’s Study Collection.

Goff’s interest in fashion design has intersected with her writing career in interesting ways. The estate of legendary costume designer Edith Head chose Goff to adapt her story for a biopic. “It’s all so surreal. I obviously have admired Edith’s work as long as I can remember, so my collection bringing this project into my life is a dream come true,” she says. Last year, Goff completed studying to become an art appraiser. She now consults in the art and auction sphere in addition to writing.

“People have been fascinated by my collection,” Goff says. “It’s a bit rare to see, frankly, collectors in this space like me. I mean like me in all sorts of ways, not just as an African American woman, but an African American woman who’s not from a privileged background. It’s important to me that I’m not the last one like me in these spaces.”

Goff spoke to ELLE about the joy of working with a museum in her Texas hometown, the old movies that inspired her love of vintage, and the designers she wishes everyone knew.

It really started by watching old movies with my mom and watching her dress up [when I was] a little girl. When I show friends old photos of her, people are always thinking, “Oh, she looks like a movie star or very Diana Ross-esque.” We would watch old movies, especially Imitation of Life and things from that era, the real glamour, the golden age of Hollywood. She would always say, “Look at the dresses, look at the dresses,” and I would. I really fell in love with old movies, which I do believe is part of how I ended up becoming a writer.

But also, I really fell in love with vintage clothes. I moved to New York and didn’t have a lot of money, and vintage was not trendy and didn’t cost thousands of dollars like it can be today. For one of my earliest jobs, I had to go to fancy events, but I had no money. I bought a couple of pieces from the ’60s at a flea market. I remember being at this event, and all these women who obviously had a lot more money to spend on clothes, asking, “Who’s this by? What boutique did you buy this at?” And I was like, “Oh, I got it at a flea market on Avenue B.” I think they thought I was joking.

I wrote a piece for The Daily Beast several years ago about the most influential Black designers in history. It was one of the most memorable pieces I’ve written. I don’t think at the time I was aware of how profoundly it impacted me, but I learned how many seminal Black American designers died of AIDS in a really short window of time. Willi Smith, one of the first Black designers to achieve major crossover commercial success in department stores, died. And so did Isaia Rankin and then Patrick Kelly. What I took away is that so much history was lost, but I also think about how different the future of American fashion might be today because these were really trailblazing and hugely influential.

They weren’t just influential Black American designers, but hugely influential American designers. Isaia Rankin basically had invented athleisure wear. It was his idea that you should be able to go from a coffee shop to a gym to the club. [He made] one of the first pieces by a Black designer I acquired online. I’ll never forget that the person selling it said, “This belonged to my aunt. Apparently, this guy used to be somebody,” which I just think is the saddest thing. He had this profound impact and then had been largely forgotten.

During the pandemic, when everyone worked from home with too much time on their hands and easy access to shop online, I ended up acquiring quite a bit, in part because a lot of the brick-and-mortar stores, particularly in Europe, were really struggling. They were so reliant on tourist foot traffic, and so a lot of them started selling online [for the first time]. And so there were a number of French boutiques I started acquiring pieces from, including some Patrick Kelly pieces that still have the original store tags from the 1980s, which I won’t remove. Those I won’t wear. The rest of them I wear when they fit. As life goes, they don’t always fit forever.

I’ve become friendly with Patrick Kelly’s widower, Bjorn Amelan, who’s a lovely, wonderful man and the keeper of Patrick’s legacy. It is important to me, when possible, to try to maintain relationships with the people I view as keepers of the legacies because I see my collection as serving the legacy of the designers. The pieces don’t belong to me. They belong to our wider community because they’re a part of our lived history.

The really cool thing is how many people I’ve met along this journey who have not only become cheerleaders but actually reach out to me about pieces. Writer Jill Kargman has become a friend and she gifted me a vintage Stephen Burrows dress. She said, “It belongs in your collection,” which is just the coolest thing ever.

I’m from Houston, and we have the Houston Museum of African American Culture here. We’re living in a really interesting time where people are having conversations about the politics of diversity, but one of the things that’s cool about fashion is that people of different political persuasions were like, “I think this collection’s really cool. I read an article about your collection, I ended up ordering a book about Elizabeth Keckley, or I ended up going down a rabbit hole about Ann Lowe.” At this moment, to be able to do an exhibition like this in my hometown felt particularly poignant.

Melanie Lawson has been a legendary anchor in Houston for decades. She was asked what she’s going to do in retirement, and she said that her husband, John Guess Jr., was the CEO of the Houston Museum of African American Culture. I sent him a note about how much Melanie inspired me and then mentioned my collection.

It was just kismet. They’ve actually never done a fashion exhibition. It was a real gamble. But what I so appreciated is that they had the same vision that, in a time in which our world is so divided, it’s really beautiful when you can find pieces of art that people can come together around.

This interview has been edited and condensed.

#6674. Jamaica Revisited: A New Expression of Caribbean Luxury

Sandals Resorts elevates its robust amenities across the properties of its home island.

There are places in the sun that are just a little more special than the rest. Jamaica is one of them, with powder-sand shores lined with luxury resorts; a dense, verdant interior laced with waterfalls and coffee farms; waters that range from the lightest turquoise to the darkest navy; and a distinctive cuisine layered with spice. The beaches are spectacular and the natural wonders such as the crystalline YS Falls and the winding Martha Brae River are just that—full of awe and adventure.

The Taíno name for Jamaica is Xaymaca, which translates to “the land of wood and water”—and few descriptions capture the island more distinctly. For Sandals Resorts, that ethos has inspired a homegrown luxury. Born in Jamaica more than four decades ago, the brand remains deeply rooted in the island’s familial spirit, personality, food, and topography, even as its properties continue to evolve beyond their birthplace. The result is an immersive travel experience shaped by beaches, lush mountains, local flavors, deep culture, and the people who make Jamaica an unforgettable destination.

From the energy of Montego Bay and Ocho Rios to the sweeping coastline of Negril and the more tranquil pockets of the South Coast, the seven Sandals resorts across Jamaica each offer distinct ways to settle into the island. Across the collection properties, accommodations function as private retreats within a bigger resort experience. Swim-Up Suites allow guests to slide directly from the terrace into the water. Private pools create an aquatic world unto themselves. And on the Caribbean Sea, the Overwater Butler Villas turn a quiet resting place above the water into a pampered vacation lifestyle.

This year, a trio of properties are entering significantly new chapters following gorgeous reimaginings. The iconic comebacks promise renewed accommodations, including new Swim-Up suites, and new dining options. Cocooned by nature thanks to its setting beside a 500-acre preserve, Sandals Jamaica South Coast reopens November 18, with Overwater Butler Villas and the brand’s first Two Queen Junior Suites—perfect for friend-group travel. One month later, December 18 sees the return of Sandals Jamaica Montego Bay, introducing a redesigned pool, Sandals Jamaica Caribbean Cay features newly refreshed accommodations, which are luxurious cocoons. Some days the hardest decision you make might be whether to head for the beach, dine at your favorite restaurant, or remain in your robe exactly where you are.

At Sandals Jamaica Montego Bay, the resort where the brand first began, renewed ocean-view suites promise an impressive vantage point to view the gorgeous ocean. The new Bay Roc Rum Club embraces the music and rum culture that’s part of the fabric of Jamaica and the Caribbean.

Nearby, the former Sandals Jamaica Royal Caribbean emerges as Sandals Jamaica Caribbean Cay with a unique resort experience centered around the sea and water. The new SkyPool Suites will feature a private plunge pool with an infinity edge that’s cantilevered from a large open air terrace, allowing guests to swim while enjoying uninterrupted views of the white sand and aqua waters below.

Further south, the secluded Sandals Jamaica South Coast offers ultra-luxury villas, including detached overwater villas arranged in a heart shape over the calm lagoon. Each comes equipped with see-through glass floor panels, outdoor overwater hammocks, and private boat dock access for the ultimate ocean-to-door service.

Jamaican food rarely arrives without presence. Scotch bonnets bring the heat, pimento adds the spice, and jerk carries the intensity of wood and smoke long before the plate lands on the table. That sense of heritage is part of the experience at Sandals Jamaica Caribbean Cay with Suppa, a new restaurant inspired by the island ritual of Sunday dinner. The menu celebrates familiar Jamaican flavors in savory dishes, stews, and curries served in a casual, supper-style setting made for sharing plates around the table. The adjoining Keynote Rum Bar features a soundtrack of the island’s legends in a laid-back lounge drenched in warm leather and rich tones, plus an extensive Caribbean rum selection.

The waterfront Buccan at Sandals Jamaica Montego Bay brings a different kind of fire. This open air space is where meats, seafood, and veggies are cooked over an open hearth and served at family-style tables set by the ocean. The well-received concept first debuted at the lush and secluded Sandals Saint Vincent, nestled in its own private cove, and is now arriving in Jamaica.

Visiting Sandals Jamaica South Coast, every beach day can start with Jamaica’s renowned Blue Mountain coffee and island pastries at BLŪM before afternoons stretch into hours at The Jerk Shack, enjoying must-have Jamaican jerk chicken, jerk pork, fish in foil, and other heritage-style comfort snacks. At the newly arrived Butch’s Island Chop House, excellent steak dinners and perfectly chilled martinis are on the menu.

Arguably one of the greatest luxuries while on a getaway is not having to weigh every decision. Sandals’ all-inclusive model is built around freedom. Not only are meals, snacks, and drinks included, but so are many of the resort experiences that turn a beach trip into an adventure, such as snorkeling, paddleboarding, kayaking, and daily diving for certified scuba divers, as well as classes to become PADI certified. Back on land, guests can move from the beach to an active day at the tennis and pickleball courts. For the golf lover, a day at Sandals Ochi, Sandals Dunn’s River, and Sandals Royal Plantation in Jamaica also include complimentary greens fees at Upton Estate Golf & Country Club in the green hills above Ocho Rios.

All-inclusive leaves room for every traveler to have their own version of the Caribbean holiday. One guest may spend the morning beneath the surface of the sea and the afternoon learning pickleball, then indulging in fresh sushi and sashimi. Another may decide the day’s only pursuit should be moving from a suite to a lounge chair, then being served jerk chicken or just-out-the-oven pizza beachside.

For all of Jamaica’s waterfalls, rivers, lagoons, beaches, and mountains, the element travelers often cherish most is a feeling of welcome. The ease of a conversation with the butler, the waiter who remembers your daily coffee order, the laugh with the bartender that extends a quick interaction into a memory, the recommendation to try a local dish, visit a secluded beach or a local shop or market that might have otherwise been missed is waiting in Jamaica.

That kind of Jamaican hospitality at Sandals cannot be engineered by simply refreshing a pool or designed into a new suite. It comes from people knowing how to welcome guests to their home. At Sandals Resorts, the flavor, the memorable landscapes, and the contagious Jamaican warmth makes visitors feel less like they simply arrived at a destination—and more like they’ll be welcomed back again and again.Book your Jamaican getaway today at sandals.com.

#6673. Simu Liu’s First Favorite Brand Was Abercrombie & Fitch

Simu Liu is no stranger to fashion’s biggest night, so, when I met him at his hotel in SoHo Monday night, he figured the Council of Fashion Designers of America Awards show should be a cinch. “I think everything’s a little bit more chill than the Met Gala,” Liu says. “So I’m looking forward to having a little bit of a more relaxed environment to talk to fashion houses and meet people from the different brands and also just to see friends.”

We speak just a few hours before the 37-year-old actor is about to make his first appearance at the Oscars of fashion and it’s hard to tell that he just hopped off a plane from Los Angeles this morning. The Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings actor has had a packed year, from making his Broadway debut in Oh, Mary! between February and April to getting married back in October. He’s preparing to start promotion for the highly anticipated December release of Avengers: Doomsday, in which he’s set to reprise his role as the superhero Shang-Chi. Marvel fans haven’t seen him on the screen since his record-breaking film debut in 2021. “It’s been a long, long time,” he jokes.

For now, he’s clad in a robe sitting barefoot on the sofa, swiping a metallic device across his unblemished, glowing face. “I think it’s like a gua sha, but it’s cold,” he speculates. (His makeup artist, Alex Keating, confirms that it’s Shark Beauty’s Depuffi, a hot-and-cold contrast therapy gua sha that basically “gives you a full facial.”) A room service trolley is sitting inches away from him, allowing him quick access to a plate of chicken tenders and fries. And a Diet Coke. Don’t forget the Diet Coke.

Keating makes good use of Liu’s wavy locks, hairspraying a Superman-like curl into permanent place on his forehead as he sips his fridge cigarette. The actor’s dad cut his hair until he was 18 and he says it took him a while to learn what worked for his own mane. He envied the typical stick-straight Asian hair others had, but through his work with groomers learned the power of salt sprays to lean into his hair’s natural texture. It admittedly took a while for Liu to develop his own fashion sense as an adult, too.

“When you grow up working class and you grow up with parents whose purchasing habits were just the furthest thing from luxurious, I think it just takes time for you to learn about fashion,” he says. “The first brand that I remember really caring about was Abercrombie & Fitch.”

Tonight, though, Liu has moved far beyond the mall. He’s attending the CFDA Awards on behalf of White Rabbit Trust, an organization that supports AAPI creatives and entrepreneurs. It's hosting the award’s Emerging Designers Table, which allows industry leaders—this year, Jason Wu—to mentor AAPI designers who create custom looks for the muse of their choosing. In Liu’s case, he’s been dressed by Asian-Canadian designer Haoran Li of the brand Private Policy.

The look for the evening was a matching set made from black silk jacquard woven with bamboo paired with a shiny new silver wedding ring and a Rolex Batman GMT-Master II. His cropped trucker-style jacket, accented by hand-knotted Chinese buttons, sat over a crisp frayed-hem white button-down with wide-legged pants that draped over low-profile black shoes. “In Chinese culture, bamboo is one of the Four Gentlemen, a symbol of integrity and resilience,” Li says. “It bends in the storm but never breaks. That felt like Simu, who has spent his career pushing through doors that weren’t built for us.”

I ask if he’s ever bothered by the responsibility of representing the Asian diaspora. “Right around the time Crazy Rich Asians came out, it was the first studio Asian movie in 25 years,” he recalls. “Then Shang-Chi was the first Asian Marvel superhero movie. For a while it was just like first this, first this, first this. So I felt like innately the stakes were high and I put pressure on myself. I don’t regret doing that. I just remember looking around and not really seeing anyone doing that. So I thought, well it might as well be me.”

To that point, this isn’t the first time Liu has used his name to promote an indie AAPI brand. At the the premiere of Shang-Chi in 2021, he spotlighted Singaporean-British designer Chelsea Scott-Blackhall’s label Dzojchen, wearing the brand’s silk kimono tuxedo.

Prominence in Hollywood has meant more to him than giving him the opportunity to wear really nice clothes. He’s decided to take more agency in his career, he says. Last year, he starred and executive produced the spy thriller series The Copenhagen Test, which despite favorable reviews was cancelled after one season. That hasn’t slowed his aspirations for new creative outlets: "I think actually right now I’m really excited by the idea of becoming a director."

But before we get to see “Directed by Simu Liu” on the big screen, the star has an awards show to attend—and a plate of tendies to devour. Just as quickly as he’s touched down here in New York, he’s off again to Hong Kong tomorrow.

#6672. A Diwali Menu That’s Full of Joy (and Sticky Chicken Wings)

Growing up, I remember a steady stream of guests coming in and out of our home in the weeks leading up to Diwali. The season would start with Navratri, a nine-night Hindu festival celebrating the divine feminine, Shakti, through the worship of Goddess Durga. Our celebrations were led by women, my grandmother, mother, and aunts, who would meticulously clean the house and spend weeks preparing snacks and sweets. They taught me the art of hosting and how to share the joy of food with our community.

I came to associate Diwali with that sense of abundance, care, and graciousness. There was always more food than we needed, and always room for more people. When I moved to New York, I started to miss that deeply, so I began a tradition to share Diwali with my chosen family here, many of whom were experiencing the holiday through food for the first time.

I’m the kind of host who likes to enjoy her own party, which means being strategic about the menu. I lean on dishes like my homestyle chicken kari, which can be made ahead and tastes even better the next day. And then there are dishes that bring a little theater to the table, like the creamy rice pudding which gets torched before serving. I want food that feeds a crowd, feels special, and lets me spend less time in the kitchen and more time with the people I love.

Guests always ask me for this crowd-pleasing app. Japanese sweet potatoes have a creamy texture that pairs beautifully with the spicy, crunchy elements of chaat. Best of all, the spuds can be cooked ahead, with the toppings added just before serving. One less thing for you to do on the big day.

Wings reign supreme when it comes to a party appetizer, and these tamarind-glazed ones deliver tangy punch in every bite. The marinade combines tamarind purée, fish sauce, brown sugar, red pepper flakes, and cumin, with extra glaze brushed on for maximum flavor and char. Be sure to finish with fried onions for bonus crunch.

This tastes like you spent hours cooking, but actually it comes together in less than an hour. The best part? It’s even better the next day, making it ideal for hosting. Gently reheat the kari before guests arrive, letting the warm, heady spices fill your home before everyone gathers around the table.

Mushrooms are an underrated ingredient in Indian cooking, and this creamy masala puts the earthy veg front and center. Sautéing them in batches gives the shrooms beautifully caramelized edges, while deglazing the pot captures all those flavorful browned bits. Serve the masala with rice or warm flatbread to sop up all the savory sauce.

No Diwali celebration is complete without something sweet, but dessert doesn’t have to be elaborate to feel special. This recipe transforms a handful of pantry staples into a rich, creamy rice pudding. For a playful twist, finish it with a crackly brûléed sugar crust and serve with a scoop of mango sorbet.

#6671. Andrew Garfield and Monica Barbaro’s Complete Relationship Timeline

Awards season brought love into Andrew Garfield’s life. On Feb. 21, 2025, People reported that Garfield has been “quietly” dating A Complete Unknown’s Monica Barbaro after the two were seen together in London.

A source told People that “they’ve been really low-key and have been spending time together quietly.” The actors’ reps did not respond to People’s request for comment.

In October 2024, Garfield told Esquire that he protects his love life, so don’t expect him to comment on any dating rumors. “I have never, and I won’t ever, speak about or confirm or deny anything about my personal life with anyone, ever,” he said.

Garfield, 43, was last romantically linked to spiritual adviser Dr. Kate Tomas; she confirmed their breakup on Oct. 11, 2024.

#6670. Pumpkin Bolognese

Classic Bolognese, with its multi-hour cook time, can be truly remarkable, if you ever have a stretch to make it. In this version, a scoop of canned pumpkin purée is the head-turning ingredient that gives it full-blown flavor and body, without the wait typical of a nonna-style sauce. Lightly caramelizing the pumpkin in the pot along with tomato paste gives it a nutty, savory edge. Milk is the other surprise ingredient here, especially in the quantity of a full cup. Think of it as a tenderizer, making the final sauce soft and delicate. Pay attention to the order in which the ingredients appear—the milk goes in first with the wine to follow. If you switch the order, the acidic wine will curdle the milk.

This recipe is part of Pumpkin Week 2026, Bon Appétit’s annual celebration of autumn’s most magical pantry staple.

Heat 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium. Add 1 large white or yellow onion, finely chopped, 2 celery stalks, finely chopped, 5 garlic cloves, finely chopped, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ¼ tsp. freshly grated nutmeg and stir to combine. Cover pot and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion and celery are very soft, 8–10 minutes. Uncover and continue to cook, stirring occasionally, until onion and celery are golden around the edges, about 5 minutes.

Uncover pot and add 1 lb. ground beef, preferably 20% fat; season lightly with salt. Cook, stirring occasionally, until beef is very lightly browned but not crisp (it will still be pink in spots), 6–8 minutes. Pour in 1 cup whole milk and cook, stirring occasionally, until milk has evaporated and fat is pooling on surface of meat, 7–10 minutes.

Pour in 1 cup dry white wine and cook, stirring occasionally, until wine has evaporated, 6–8 minutes. Add 1 cup canned pumpkin purée and 2 Tbsp. double-concentrated tomato paste; season generously with freshly ground pepper. Cook, stirring often and scraping bottom of pot, until combined and pumpkin darkens slightly, 8–10 minutes.

Pour in 1 cup water, reduce heat to low, and cook, stirring occasionally, until mixture is saucy, 12–15 minutes. If meat seems dry, add an extra ½ cup water and continue cooking another 3–4 minutes. Taste sauce and season with salt if needed. Keep warm.

Meanwhile, cook 12 oz. fresh tagliatelle or pappardelle or dry rigatoni, in a large pot of boiling salted water. If using fresh pasta, cook about 3 minutes. If using dry, cook until very al dente, about 2 minutes less than package directions.

Using tongs, transfer pasta to pot with sauce. Add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid and 2 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about 1 cup). Increase heat to medium, bring to a simmer, and cook, tossing constantly, until pasta is al dente and sauce is slightly thickened, about 2 minutes.

Transfer pasta to shallow bowls and sprinkle with more Parmesan.

#6669. 23 Iconic ’90s Bobs, as Seen on Celebrities

Few eras maintain the same grip on our imagination as the 1990s. A last gasp before the rise of social media, the decade feels even more fun, raucous, and carefree. Just look at the beauty trends: eyebrows tweezed to within an inch of their lives. Thick lashings of black eyeliner and cheeks devoid of blush. Brown lip liner and frosted pastel eye shadow everywhere. Plus, a hair look that feels current now (and never truly went away in the interim): the bob haircut.

The beauty of the ’90s bob specifically is that it tended to mean something slightly different depending on the wearer. Naomi Campbell embraced the razor-cut bob—a super-short, symmetrical cut that fell on either side of her face, with bumped-under ends. The then Posh Spice made the longer bob her calling card, and Christy Turlington cemented the blown-out glamour of the supermodel bob.

Below, 24 of our favorite bobs from the decade we never tire of looking back on.

#6667. 25 Great Gifts for New Dads, According to GQ

Becoming a dad changes a lot of things. Your sleep schedule, for one. Your relationship with a clean shirt, for another. But just because a guy has entered his daddy era doesn't mean he's stopped caring about the things he cared about before.

With that in mind, we've rounded up the best gifts for new dads, with a little something for him and the little one. Some are practical things that'll make those early days of fatherhood a little easier. Others are simply things that'll make him feel good, look good, and a little more like himself.

Nothing doing? Check out the rest of our gift guides and sign up for the GQ Recommends newsletter for more gift ideas worth your money.

At some point, he'll emerge back into the world, and there's nothing like a great shirt to ease the reentry. This swaggy checked shirt from Beams has all the layering built right in, so he can look like he hasn't missed a step.

There's a lot to be said for clothes that don't require much thought, especially when you've got a new bundle. Take this double-faced merino wool bomber from Quince: warm, unfussy, and easy to throw on with just about anything.

Some brands really are thinking of the children. Everybody.World makes its Trash Zip Hoodie from 100% recycled cotton waste, giving discarded material a second life as a very good sweatshirt.

A good pair of sweatpants is nonnegotiable. From the true masters of the category, these midweight terry sweatpants from Reigning Champ come with a relaxed silhouette, an open hem, and a nicely lived-in patina.

The undisputed king of dad shoes has entered its seventh generation, with its first major redesign since 2022 bringing a sleeker suede-and-mesh upper, softer cushioning, and all the Made in USA pedigree you'd expect. For a guy who's just become a dad, the timing couldn't be better.

He's a dad now. A man of refinement, responsibility, and a pressing need for a do-it-all boot. Enter Blundstone's new Heritage boot, a top-shelf take on its legendary shit-stomper, upgraded with premium leather and Goodyear-welted construction.

The baby's developing a sense of sight, and there's no reason for dad to sacrifice his. Lalo's Play Gym II is a far better-looking alternative to what's out there, with plenty to keep little hands and eyes occupied, including sensory toys, teethers, and a bell. The brand's set of high-contrast art cards wouldn't hurt, either.

If they've already got a Tripp Trapp, this one's a no-brainer. The iconic high chair is part of MoMA's permanent collection, and now the museum's Design Store has a set of colorful cushions to go with it.

One thing new parents can never have enough of is a good place to put the baby down. Part quilt, part playmat, these organic cotton numbers from House of Noa are among the most handsome we've seen, with an heirloom quality that makes 'em worth holding on to long after the baby has outgrown tummy time.

The problem with BabyBjörn? Too many good things to choose from. But for new parents, the gift of a few hands-free minutes is hard to beat. The new Bouncer Begin is designed specifically for newborns, with a shallower seat than the brand's wildly popular Bouncer Bliss.

Bottle-washing is a dad duty. We don't make the rules. Baby Brezza's Bottle Washer Pro 360 makes the job considerably less miserable, washing, sterilizing, and drying bottles in one go.

Two things you can never have enough of with a newborn: muslin and blankets. Coyuchi's wonderfully soft muslin quilt takes care of both.

New dads live by the clock. Three hours between feeds, 20 minutes until the next nap, two minutes to themselves, if they're lucky. Braun's Time Teacher, with its clean, easy-to-read dial, colorful hands, and markings for phrases like "quarter past" and "half past," makes keeping track a little easier. And when the little one is old enough to tell time, it'll come in handy all over again.

Apple's finally getting into the smart display game. The new HomeView is the company's first dedicated smart home hub, bringing home controls, FaceTime, and the usual Apple ecosystem conveniences to one ittle screen. Its 12-megapixel camera should come in especially handy for keeping the grandparents supplied with baby sightings.

A sleeping baby is a beautiful thing. Hatch's portable Go sound machine is a little godsend, with soothing sounds, a rechargeable battery, and a handy clip for attaching it to the stroller or car seat.

Bose's new sport-minded open earbuds let him enjoy his music or a podcast without tuning out what's happening around him—like, say, an actual human baby. And on the rare occasion he gets out for a run, they'll be just as useful for logging a few miles.

For the dad with his hands full (read: all dads), Ray-Ban's Meta Zena glasses pair a snazzy cat-eye silhouette with the ability to capture first steps, film stroller outings, or video-call the grandparents, all without reaching for his phone.

Tiny Vinyl's miniature record player and four-inch records are pure novelty, but there's something rather charming about a tiny turntable for a tiny human. Start building the little one's record collection now, and they'll have something to grow into.

Fujifilm's new Instax Pal 2 gives dad another way to document his little one, packing a digital camera into an adorable, palm-sized package. He can send shots straight to his phone, or pair it with an Instax printer for a few keepsakes the grandparents can stick on the fridge.

there's something to be said for having a few memories you can actually hold in your hands. This new 35mm point-and-shoot from Kodak lets him capture the little one on film, with actual prints to show for it.

Coterie diapers really do live up to the hype. And the brand's skincare lineup is pretty terrific, too. This set brings together full-size bottles of its hair and body wash, all-over moisturizer, and diaper and dry skin balm.

Dad's going to need all the help he can get in the sleep department. No surprise there. What might surprise him is how much magnesium can help, from supporting normal muscle and nerve function to regulating the body's stress response and potentially improving sleep quality.

The Fitbit Air might be the sleekest screen-free fitness tracker around, and at a price that makes it an easy sell. For the new dad who just wants to keep tabs on his sleep and daily steps without getting too deep into the fitness-data weeds, it's a straightforward proposition.

A little time for some om-ing is a fine idea for any new dad. Walden's meditation set gives him a dedicated place to find his center, and the accompanying mat doubles as a nice spot for the little one to stretch out.

#6666. Pumpkin Enchiladas With Black Beans

Homemade enchiladas might sound like a laborious weekend project, but with a few clever tricks, this version made with black beans and pumpkin can be whipped up on even the most hurried of work nights. For starters, canned pumpkin creates the base of a quick sauce that requires no precooking. And because they are vegetarian, the filling—a combination of canned black beans, onion, and bell pepper flecked with cilantro—comes together in a flash. In lieu of baking the enchiladas, this version opts for broiling in order to brown the tops while also heating the enchiladas through in the same skillet you cook the beans in. A flourish of pumpkin seeds, sliced onion, cilantro, and fresh lime brightens up everything, although serving them straight from the oven would be just as delicious.

This recipe is part of Pumpkin Week 2026, Bon Appétit’s annual celebration of autumn’s most magical pantry staple.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large broilerproof skillet over medium-high. Add 1 large white onion, finely chopped, and 1 medium green bell pepper, halved, ribs and seeds removed, finely chopped, and cook, stirring often, until browned in spots and fragrant, 7–9 minutes. Add 4 garlic cloves, finely grated, two 15-oz. cans black beans, rinsed, and 2 Tbsp. chili powder and cook, stirring occasionally, just until combined and beans are warmed through, about 3 minutes. Transfer bean mixture to a large bowl; reserve pan.

Smash bean mixture with a spoon or potato masher until about half of the beans are mashed. Mix in juice of 1 lime and ¼ cup coarsely chopped cilantro; season with kosher salt. Set bean mixture aside.

Whisk together one 15-oz. can pumpkin purée, 1 tsp. Tabasco, and 1¼ cups water in a large bowl; season pumpkin sauce with salt.

Place 1 of twelve 6" flour tortillas on a surface. Scoop out ¼ cup (heaping) reserved bean mixture and arrange in center down length of tortilla. Scatter some of 4 oz. pepper jack cheese or sharp cheddar, coarsely grated (about ¾ cup), over, then roll up tortilla into a cylinder. Place, seam side down, in reserved skillet. Repeat process with remaining tortillas. Brush tops with oil.

Place a rack in upper third of oven; heat broiler. Broil enchiladas until tops are deeply toasted and charred in spots, 4–7 minutes (depending on your broiler; watch carefully as they can go from browned to burnt very quickly). Pour pumpkin sauce over enchiladas and spread into an even layer. Top with remaining 4 oz. pepper jack cheese or sharp cheddar, coarsely grated (about ¾ cup) and raw pumpkin seeds (pepitas; if using). Broil until cheese is melted and deeply browned in spots, 4–7 minutes (watch carefully). Remove enchiladas from broiler and top with thinly sliced white onion and cilantro leaves with tender stems. Serve with lime wedges for squeezing over.

#6665. Cranberry Meringue Pie

A big, billowing cloud of meringue tops this crimson beauty and acts as a sweet reprieve from the tart cranberry curd. The vibrant filling is made even more sour with a generous amount of lime juice. Think lemon meringue pie but holiday-ified. Use our Perfect Pie Crust as the base to create a sturdy-flaky foundation, and be sure to start the pie the day before you plan to serve it, as the curd requires several hours of chilling to set into a sliceable texture. Cut into it too soon and it will run onto your plate, creating a messy—albeit delicious—slice.

We never make pie dough without a metal bench scraper. Our favorite is from Gestura. Use the scraper to cut butter, fold dough and nudge it into shape, transfer it from counter to plastic wrap, trim edges, cut strips, and, sure, scrape flour off your counter.

Welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

3 hours (plus 30 minutes for freezing and 5 hours for chilling)

Whisk 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ¼ tsp. baking powder in a large bowl to combine. Add 2 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces, and rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 10 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash with your fingers into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea-size).

Make a well in the center of mixture and pour in ¼ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute, then knead in bowl a couple of times to bring dough together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn out dough onto a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour and dust top of dough with flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold dough in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting with more rice flour as needed to prevent sticking. Pat into a ½"-thick disk and wrap tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Let dough disk sit at room temperature 5 minutes. Roll out dough on a lightly floured surface to a 12" round, about ¼" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and wrap around rolling pin. Transfer to a 9"-diameter pie pan (such as East Fork Spun Iron Pie Dish). Unfurl into pan, then lift edges and allow dough to slump down into pan. Trim, leaving about a 1½" overhang. Fold overhang under so crust is flush with edges of pan and crimp as desired with lightly floured fingers. Set pan on a rimmed baking sheet and prick bottom and sides of crust with a fork in several places. Freeze, uncovered, at least 30 minutes and up to 2 hours.

Place a rack in lower third of oven; preheat to 400°. Line crust with a sheet of parchment paper and fill with pie weights or dried beans. Bake crust, tenting edges with foil if browning too quickly, until edges are set and look dry, 20–25 minutes. Carefully lift out parchment paper and weights and continue baking crust, gently pressing bottom and sides occasionally with a flat-bottomed measuring cup if puffing up, until bottom looks dry and is golden, 20–25 minutes more. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let crust cool.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

Bring 1 lb. fresh or frozen cranberries, 1½ cups (300 g) granulated sugar, and ¼ cup water to a boil in a large saucepan, then reduce heat to medium and simmer, stirring often, until cranberries soften and burst and most of the liquid has evaporated, 10–15 minutes. Let cranberry mixture cool.

Transfer cranberry mixture to a blender; reserve pan. Add ⅔ cup fresh lime juice and ¼ cup (32 g) cornstarch and blend on high speed until smooth. Scrape purée back into pan (not over heat) and add 3 large eggs, 2 large egg yolks, 1 Tbsp. vanilla extract, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Place over medium heat and cook, whisking constantly, until mixture bubbles and thickens to a pudding-like consistency, about 4 minutes. Remove pan from heat. Add ¾ cup (1½ sticks) unsalted butter, room temperature, cut into pieces, and whisk until melted and combined. Strain curd through a fine-mesh sieve, pushing with a rubber spatula, directly into crust. Smooth into an even layer and cover with plastic wrap, pressing directly onto surface. Chill pie at least 4 hours and up to 1 day.

Just before serving, beat 6 large egg whites, room temperature, ¼ tsp. cream of tartar, remaining 1¼ cups (250 g) granulated sugar, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment on medium speed until foamy and sugar is dissolved, about 5 minutes. Increase speed to high and continue to beat until stiff peaks form, about 3 minutes more.

Spoon meringue over filling and swirl decoratively as desired. Using a kitchen torch, toast meringue if desired.

#6664. Exclusive: The All’s Fair Cast Held Court in Couture at the Season 2 Premiere and After-Party

“This season is just more of everything,” Kim Kardashian told Vogue, as Sarah Paulson shrieked “Yes!” in agreement, adding, “More drama, more sex, more fun, more fashion, more shenanigans.” They were talking, of course, about All’s Fair, Ryan Murphy’s panache-packed Hulu series following high-powered divorce attorneys with silver tongues, scores to settle, and exceptionally good wardrobes to do it in. On Monday, the cast gathered on Manhattan’s West Side for the New York premiere of season two, the third installment of their whistle-stop publicity tour.

Much like in the series itself, there was no shortage of drama at the Highline Studios: white velvet ropes, marble, and an infinite amount of gold. Add to that the parade of couture emerging from black cars, and suddenly the first Monday in November seemed as glamorous as a certain Monday in May. “This is All’s Fair! You either go big or go home,” quipped hairstylist Sharif Poston while giving Niecy Nash-Betts’s hair a final once-over with a shiny metallic comb.

The show’s costuming certainly sets the precedent for such excess. Fred Leighton brooches, Balenciaga gowns, and no shortage of Birkins. “The show’s wardrobe has the biggest budget I’ve ever seen,” revealed actress Denise Richards. “I was actually quite impressed by it.” (And that’s coming from a former Bond girl.)

For this red-carpet outing, some went the lawyerly route, while others dialed up the haute factor. Teyana Taylor managed to tick both boxes in an architectural Nicholas Oakwell Couture pantsuit, festooned with a giant bow below the waist. Her summation of the evening was the same as hers of the second season: “It’s drama and suits!” Similarly, actor Nyle DiMarco nodded to the legal theme in a Paul Smith suit, “straight off the runway.” And Nash-Betts’s Louis Vuitton look had multiple acts. “This dress turns into three or four different things—so keep your eyes on me.” Sure enough, the next time I saw her, the gilded halo that initially framed her was nowhere to be seen.

“She looks so good,” director and executive producer Anthony Hemingway said as Kardashian arrived in a lace-up Ashi Studio gown with a sweetheart neckline and a snatched bodice, accentuated with lace, croc embossing, and ribbons. Everyone seemed to stand a little straighter as Kardashian walked in—but sure enough, as soon as she started chatting, the room relaxed.

“I’m excited for people to see how funny we are,” Kardashian said. “There’s a lot more comedy this season,” Paulson added, hooking a thumb toward Kardashian, who leaned right into it. “I’m the funniest,” she teased. Paulson had her own theory: “Kim did a movie with all these comedy geniuses in between seasons one and two,” she said, explaining that her co-star came back to set brimming with notes. When Paulson said she’s still waiting for Saturday Night Live to call, Kardashian chimed in with an idea of her own: “Should we do it together? Please!”

Though there were photos to take and interviews to give, the cast still stopped mid-carpet for a catch-up. Glenn Close, in Matières Fécales, had missed the first two stops on the press tour. “I’m excited to see my friends,” she said, holding hands with Kardashian through an entire interview. Taylor, who’d been busy wrapping up another project as director, felt much the same. “You have to understand the FOMO I’ve been having.”

“We had long TV days that lasted up to sixteen hours sometimes,” Naomi Watts added. “It’s a grind, but we somehow find a way to laugh in between takes.” She credited Murphy with putting together a group that clicked. “There’s not an outsized ego amongst us.” For Taylor, that sisterhood mattered especially on the days she turned up feeling less than her best. “Everybody’s got their silent battles,” she said. “Come to work with them, and with this cast, you just know that you’re going to be surrounded by love.”

For reality TV regular Dorinda Medley, who plays Loni and worked mostly with Glenn Close, taking on a scripted role was a chance to try something new. “All these little steps in your life move you a little closer to who you are,” she said. “For so many years I was Dorinda someone.” She ticked off the surnames she’d gone by and the roles she’d played offscreen. “Mother, wife, widow. Now, for the first time, I’m just Dorinda. There’s incredible freedom in that.” Medley, in an embellished Gucci dress that she jokingly called “very casual,” already had a pitch for her next collaboration with Murphy. How about setting American Horror Story at Blue Stone Manor, her home in the Berkshires?

“We rarely get a chance to rock together. We’re always working,” Hemingway, the director, said. He was looking forward to a chance to “hang out, have a cocktail, even do a little two-step, and just laugh.” And at Crane Club nearby, there was ample opportunity for all four. Around the red velvet-draped dining room, servers made the rounds with truffle arancini and caesar salads, a giant ice sculpture of the show’s initials presided over the raw bar, and the DJ was good enough to make you forget it was a school night.

If the carving station said wedding reception, the cocktail menu said divorce. Bartenders whipped up drinks named Contested Assets, with habanero-spiked mezcal number, and Alimony, which came with gin, vodka, vermouth, sake, and a little cucumber. Taylor had a special order in mind. “I need a real big margarita,” she told Vogue. Her favorite? “Passionfruit. Sugar rim. There—you’ve got sugar, spice, and everything nice,” she said, dancing as she delivered the recipe.

For a cast that had reserved tables ringing the room, they sure spent little time in their seats. And who could blame them? Ash Hodgkinson was doing magic tricks for a knot of guests, while Murphy, in ochre-tinted aviators, made duck faces for the camera with Paulson. When the DJ put on “Plain Jane,” there was Nash-Betts, dancing with her girls. “I love those moments,” Hemingway had said. “That’s living.”

As for any flak the show had received, Anna Delvey, who knows a thing or two about mixed press and courthouse fashion, had a thought. “It says a lot about people, how they take it,” she explained—stating that some people “are too serious about it.” In her view, anyone busy cataloging the show’s excesses was liable to miss the joke. “They obviously know what they’re doing,” she said of the silliness.

#6663. The Midi Bob Is the Sleek, High-Shine Haircut That Flatters 50-Plus Hair

This elegant style will be everywhere this fall.

Finding a hairstyle more sought-after than a well-cut midi bob (a long bob that brushes the shoulders or collarbones but delivers a blunt, full effect) is no small feat. Favored by celebrities such as Pamela Anderson, Halle Berry, Hailey Bieber, Kaia Gerber, and Julianne Moore, this shoulder-grazing style has become something of a signature among A-listers in recent years. Coincidentally, it is also one of the most flattering cuts for anyone over 50.

Most recently, Claudia Winkleman has brought the midi bob back into the spotlight, as her bold signature hairstyle continues to make headlines as the Celebrity Traitors hits screens.

As the name suggests, the lob offers a middle ground between long hair and a bob. It falls anywhere between the chin and the collarbone and is often seen as a transitional style for those looking to go shorter gradually.

“Hitting just at the collarbone, the lob offers the best of both worlds: the ease of a bob with the styling flexibility of longer hair,” says Elliot Bute, hairstylist at Hershesons Fitzrovia. “It’s incredibly versatile, particularly for anyone who wants the ease of a shorter haircut but still wants to be able to tie their hair back.”

He adds that the cut works across most face shapes because you can adjust where the length sits and where you introduce layers or movement. Take Julianne Moore, for example. Her blunt cut creates glossy fullness in her natural hair, while fellow actor Winona Ryder has adopted the style in a more undone, choppy way.

Remember, depending on your lob style, your styling routine will look different, as Tim Scott-Wright, owner of Tim Scott-Wright at The Hair Surgery, explains here.

“The lob is a strong, on-trend look that is great with a wave,” he says. “It’s kind of an in-between look and is best worn wavy with texture. It’s a way of modernizing lacklustre long hair without losing all your length. Cate Blanchett and Reese Witherspoon have both recently sported this look.”

Consider investing in a texture spray or air-dry cream if your hair has natural shape and movement, or use a curling tong or straightener to create soft, natural bevels.

#6662. Ralph Lauren’s 17 Best Outfits of All Time

On Monday night, the Council of Fashion Designers of America crowned Ralph Lauren as its menswear designer of the year—his 12th win since the show’s inaugural ceremony in 1981, minting him as the most decorated designer in CFDA history. The council even has a tradition of creating awards in Lauren’s honor, as they did with the Fashion Legend Award in 2007 and the CFDA Members Salute in 2018.

At age 87, Lauren is the consummate businessman of American fashion, and he’s still producing masterclass-caliber collections that build upon his label’s established codes. In addition to his business savvy and keen eye for tailoring, the designer remains as relevant as ever in 2026 because of something far more ineffable: a deep-rooted sense of personal style. For Lauren, clothes aren’t just a wardrobe; they are identity. His own relationship with getting dressed, from his deep and abiding love of Westernwear to his knack for blending Waspy blazers with rugged workwear and military pieces, has always been at the core of everything he does. Here are some of his best looks from the last 50 years.

Technical hiking gear was a relatively late addition to the RL oeuvre, but the man was wearing hikers in the city long before hipsters discovered Salomons.

Like a skilled party DJ, Ralph Lauren has an uncanny knack for combining unlikely elements—like a yachtsman’s sweater and a pair of worn-in blue jeans—with complete ease.

There’s black-tie, and then there’s RL black-tie. There’s no doubt that Lauren can wear a pair of tuxedo pants and patent leather shoes as well as anyone, but he is much more himself in jeans and cowboy boots.

A two-year stint at Baruch College in Manhattan was the closest Lauren came to the Ivy League, but that didn’t stop him from adopting repp ties, Oxford collar shirts, and other hallmarks of the East Coast elite. The juxtaposition of oversized aviator shades with this solidly trad look is quintessential Ralph.

Think a funky belt can’t be the defining element of an otherwise understated fit? Lauren would respectfully disagree.

Few people will ever look as good in a biker jacket as Ralph Lauren did at age 70. The difference is in the details—the flannel shirt unbuttoned and tucked, the crisp white henley—and the confidence.

Lauren is a master editor, but the magic of his greatest looks is in details like a vest tucked into trousers, a knotted belt, and a pair of precisely rolled sleeves.

Yacht club up top, honkey tonk downstairs. Another Lauren signature.

Ralph Lauren never learned how to sew, but he has an instinctive understanding of tailoring. By blending the stiff silhouettes of Savile Row with the breezy swagger of American ivy style, he created a look that was all his own.

Style is all about understanding the rules before you can break them. Lauren certainly does, and that’s why this ensemble—from the wide-spread collar and slim tie combination to the double-down on stripes—works as well as it does.

There’s perhaps no more challenging look to pull off than “office cowboy,” but Ralph Lauren makes it look easy.

Leather pants and a denim shirt under a tweed jacket is another decidedly advanced maneuver, but (if executed correctly) a potentially powerful one.

In recent decades, Lauren has increasingly swapped his signature cowboy boots for La Sportiva hikers, anointing gorpcore in the process.

Lauren has always revered the look of traditional British tailoring, from safari suits to Savile Row, but he’s just as likely to pair his flannel suits with cashmere turtlenecks and cowboy boots as neckties and Oxfords.

#6661. Earthy Neutral Jeans Make Cold-Weather Outfits Feel Instantly Warmer

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

A richer alternative to classic blue denim, from cocoa wide-legs to sage straight-legs.

Listen, we love classic blue denim, but as fashion obsessives, we also believe in changing things up. If you want to drift away from black and indigo this season, consider jeans in earthy neutrals to bring a fresh outlook to your fall and winter wardrobe. The palette runs wide: chocolaty browns, soft sands, light stone blues, olive, rust, sage, and even dusty pink.

In addition to their warmth, what we love about these shades is how easily they work. Think of them as neutrals with more personality: a pair of cocoa wide-legs looks sharp with a cream turtleneck and loafers, while sage straight-legs soften an oversize charcoal blazer. Look for a rich, slightly variable dye and a sturdy cotton twill that will hold its shape and fade gracefully, then style them as you would your favorite blues, with a little more intention and a lot more warmth.

Below, we’ve rounded up some of the best earth-toned jeans to pair with your favorite fall/winter pieces.

These jeans in a cool-toned brown called “Washed Canteen Clean” pair a highly versatile earth-toned shade with a flared hem. Wear them with your favorite purple-toned knit and black ankle boots for a look that feels moody, polished, and effortlessly autumnal.

This relaxed straight-leg silhouette has a vintage-inspired shape that feels thoroughly modern, done in a light, marbled khaki wash.

Along with a wide-leg silhouette, this pair in the shade Great Basin, a hue reminiscent of muddy waters, brings a rich, moody depth to your denim rotation. Style them with a cobalt cable-knit and tan suede boots for a tonal look that feels on-trend and a little rugged.

Drawstring toggles at both hems add a subtle, unexpected sporty detail (hence the name) to a relaxed jean. Team them with your favorite court sneakers for an elevated athletic-leaning look.

In the shade “Tobacco,” these jeans are built to last a lifetime. The wide-leg fit and timeless color will earn a spot in your rotation all year long.

Barrel-leg jeans continue to be popular this season, yet this soft sepia shade trades the trend’s usual denim blue for a softer, warmer, more grounded take. Pair them with a fitted black bodysuit and pointed-toe boots to balance the roomy shape with something sleek.

Something about this shape and earthy shade brings a sense of calm and ease to our hectic everyday lives. It’s the perfect jean for slipping into a relaxed, weekend mindset.

Made of soft-stretch denim, this brown jean features a high-waisted, straight-leg shape that flatters without feeling restrictive. Style it with a tucked-in white tee, a shearling coat, and loafers for a polished, easy outfit that works from the office to the weekend.

A barrel leg in a vintage-inspired brown wash gives these jeans a lived-in, worn-in feel from the very first wear. Style them with a slim ribbed tank, a cropped leather jacket, and sling-back flats to keep the roomy shape looking sharp.

When you think of an everyday jean, perhaps the color army green doesn’t immediately come to mind. But once you see how versatile this shade can be, it’s determined to win a permanent spot in your rotation.

This slim palazzo jean brings ’70s vibes and softness to a fall color palette. Wear it with a rust-colored turtleneck, a tan suede jacket, and platform boots for a retro-leaning outfit that feels warm, confident, and distinctly seasonal.

#6660. No-Knead Pumpkin Focaccia

For those who fall into the pumpkin-should-be-savory camp, let us offer up a new recipe primed to become a seasonal staple: Pumpkin Focaccia. The iconic bread we know and love is ripe for the pumpkin treatment, lending it a golden hue and earthy sweetness. This version doesn’t require any kneading, making it straightforward enough to pull off in a single afternoon. You’ll perform a series of folds as it rises, simply pulling and stretching the dough to help it develop gluten. A showering of fresh rosemary and flaky salt on top is optional, but it takes crisp, plush focaccia from good to great. Serve it with a bowl of olive oil for dipping or a schmear of cream cheese to lean into the seasonal profile.

This recipe is part of Pumpkin Week 2026, Bon Appétit’s annual celebration of autumn’s most magical pantry staple.

Mix one ¼-oz. envelope active dry yeast (about 2¼ tsp.), 5 cups (625 g) all-purpose flour, 1 cup canned pumpkin purée, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 Tbsp. light brown sugar, and 1½ cups warm water in a large bowl until a dry, shaggy dough forms. Cover with plastic wrap and let sit in a warm spot 15 minutes.

Place a small bowl of room-temperature water on work surface for easy reaching. Uncover dough and moisten hands in water, shaking off excess. Stretch 1 side of dough up and over to meet opposite side; turn bowl 90°. Repeat process 3 more times, turning bowl after each fold. (This constitutes 1 full fold.) If dough doesn’t always stretch to meet opposite side, just aim for the middle. Remoisten your hands and shake off excess water any time dough begins to feel sticky. Cover dough and let sit 30 minutes (set a timer). Repeat entire process 2 more times (folding and resting), about 1 hour more. By the last full fold, the dough should be significantly smoother and tighter.

Pour ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil into a 13x9" metal baking pan. Lightly oil your hands and punch down dough, then transfer to prepared pan. Sprinkle with flaky sea salt. Turn dough salted side down to coat both sides in oil. Press into an even layer with your fingers. Cover with plastic wrap and let sit in a warm spot until puffy, about 45 minutes.

Place a rack in bottom third of oven; preheat to 450°. Unwrap focaccia and scatter rosemary leaves and more sea salt over if desired; drizzle with oil. Oil your hands and press fingers into focaccia several times to create dimples across surface, making sure to press fingers all the way down to the bottom of the pan. Bake focaccia, rotating pan front to back halfway through, until deep golden brown, 23–28 minutes. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let focaccia cool slightly in pan. Using a metal spatula, turn out focaccia onto rack and let cool completely.

Do Ahead: Focaccia can be made 1 day ahead. Store tightly wrapped at room temperature.
