#6659. Everything We Know About The Batman: Part II Thanks to… Heidi Klum?

If you’d told me even a month ago we’d get significant spoilers for The Batman: Part II, the next Robert Pattinson-led Batman movie, in a photo Heidi Klum posted for her annual Halloween costume, I would find that both weirdly specific and entirely unbelievable.

And yet, that looks to be exactly what happened this past weekend when prosthetics supplier The Makeup Armoury posted BTS photos of the work prosthetics expert Mike Marino (who also worked to transform Colin Farrell into The Penguin for the first film and subsequent HBO Max series) was doing for Klum. If you’ve somehow been off-grid for the last few years, you may have missed that the famed supermodel takes Halloween incredibly seriously, frequently donning costumes with extensive makeup and designs that make her unrecognizable. This year was no exception, but it might have gone largely unnoticed had that photo not accidentally revealed clues about the upcoming superhero sequel, which is currently in production with an expected release date of February 18th, 2028.

In the photo, Marino, who provided a helping, ahem, hand in Klum’s costume together for the year, had a number of molds lingering in the background, which have seemingly confirmed that Brian Tyree Henry will play Two-Face, Sebastian Stan will play Victor Zsasz, and that Part II will feature the famed Court of Owls.

Henry’s mold appears to show the Atlanta actor with a disfigured face that mimics the iconic villain. Some, including me, in this very outlet, have, speculated that he might be playing either Dent or Detective Harvey Bullock, a hardened Gotham City cop who frequently works alongside Jim Gordon. But this seems to confirm it. Considering writer-director Matt Reeves has cited Jeph Loeb and Tim Sale’s The Long Halloween as an influence on his version of the Caped Crusader, it’s not ultimately a huge surprise, but perhaps a slight disappointment considering Reeves had stated his intention to move the sequel into uncharted territory by featuring a villain that had “never really been done in a film before.”

Which brings us to Victor Zsasz, who Stan seems to be playing. There was some speculation when he shaved his head upon joining the production he might be playing the character, but the cast looks to confirm the speculation. While the serial killer—who carves tally marks into his body for every person he’s killed—shows up in Batman Begins as a minor enforcer in Carmine Falcone’s crew, he’s got a much larger role in the comic books themselves. In Long Halloween, Zsasz is hired by Falcone to assassinate Dent before he's intercepted by Batman. Might Reeves look to flip the script here and disfigure Henry’s Dent in the process? This interpretation of Zsasz would certainly fit the extremely grounded approach Reeves took in the first installment. But there’s also some confusion here, as Stan was rumored to be playing Harvey when casting first broke and even went so far as to say he’d be playing the role in an interview over the summer. The French publication Le Journal du Dimanche did, however, later retract his statement.

The last accidental spoiler is a big scoop for comic book fans. Simply labeled “Owl 3,” this likely confirms that the Court of Owls will finally make their silver-screen debut. Created in 2012 by writer Scott Snyder and artist Greg Capullo, the Owls are one of the biggest new additions to the Batman canon in recent memory. The Court is a clandestine criminal society made up of Gotham’s wealthiest and most influential citizens, whose power and influence stretch back to the city’s earliest days. They have immeasurable resources and frequently deploy assassins, known as Talons, to do their bidding. This tracks with the story Reeves told in The Batman of a Gotham beset by a history of corruption. Owls are also bats' natural predators; so that, too, is bad news for Battinson.

While this potential leak is exciting and unexpected, it also raises doubts about the identity of Scarlett Johansson’s character, as she was rumored to be playing Harvey’s wife, Gilda Dent. Either way, never in a million lifetimes could we have guessed that Heidi Klum would be the one to spill the beans about one of the most anticipated comic book movies of the next few years.

#6657. Cemeteries Are the Unsung Hero of Travel

I was flipping through old journals recently and came across an entry dated December 31, 2017. I was in Todos Santos and had risen early to watch the sunrise over the Sierra de la Laguna mountains. There were scribbled goals for the new year, and reflections on what I wanted to leave behind. But the part that stood out most was a slice of the surrounding atmosphere—rooster crows echoing in the streets, and sunlight spilling onto a colorful cemetery in the distance. It reminded me that for as long as I’ve been traveling, I’ve always sought out the local cemetery. And it’s always left an indelible impression.

If you’re not a fellow taphophile, allow me to make the case. Spending time in cemeteries invites you to sink in. It sticks your mortality front and center and reminds you that you won’t always be here (stress!). It’s also a reminder to appreciate today, and remember those who aren’t around anymore. And as it pertains to visiting the dearly departed while traveling, cemetery strolls offer a distinct way to familiarize yourself with the local people. How a culture approaches death conveys a great deal. (In the case of Mexico, graveyards are not somber, but rather, awash in rainbow colors and elaborate decorations. Very lively!)

On a less morbid note, cemeteries are also really lovely for architecture and natural landscapes. History, too. And with the spooky season in full swing (which I’d argue lasts well beyond Halloween), there’s never been a better time to become a cemetery convert. Below, nine destinations worth planning a trip around.

I’m very lucky to live less than 10 minutes from this world-famous cemetery in Brooklyn. Green-Wood was founded in 1838 and is now a National Historic Landmark. Its paths stretch across 478 hilly acres, winding beside tombs belonging to iconic figures such as Jean-Michel Basquiat and Leonard Bernstein. It’s also a Revolutionary War historic site, and a haven for birdwatchers (over 260 species have been spotted).

When I lived in Los Angeles, outdoor movie screenings at Hollywood Forever Cemetery were a common occurrence. But despite being one of the trendiest ways to spend a Saturday night, this cemetery dates back to 1899. It serves as the final resting place for numerous Hollywood legends, from Judy Garland and Cecil B. DeMille to Eve Babitz. There’s even a cenotaph marker for Toto from The Wizard of Oz for fans to memorialize the adored cairn terrier.

Established in 1821, this breathtaking cemetery features an array of architectural styles, including Neo-Gothic, Neo-Maya, and even Art Deco. Its tree- and mausoleum-lined avenues are home to over 25,000 burial sites, including Felipe Carrillo Puerto (a progressive champion of human rights who was assassinated in 1924). Leading up to Día de Los Muertos, there is a festive procession called Paseo de las Ánimas that begins at the cemetery.

I’ll preface this with the unfortunate fact that Lafayette Cemetery No. 1 is currently closed to the public (reopening is still TBD). But that doesn’t stop me from declaring it my favorite in New Orleans. This 19th-century cemetery has appeared in films such as Interview With the Vampire and can still be enjoyed with a stroll around its scenic perimeter—which is punctuated by towering Spanish live oaks whose massive roots pry the concrete curb upward into a wonderfully spooky, uneven pathway. (If you’d like to go inside a New Orleans cemetery, don’t miss voodoo practitioner Marie Laveau’s tomb in St. Louis Cemetery No. 1).

This is the cemetery I’ve probably returned to the most over the years (and arguably the most famous in the world). It’s huge, so you’ll need to set aside an entire afternoon to explore its 110 acres that play host to thousands of burial plots. Also in the thousands: trees (about 5,000), making this landscape exceptionally beautiful as the leaves change colors. Don’t miss the highlights—Jim Morrison, Frédéric Chopin, Oscar Wilde, Édith Piaf—but also give yourself time to wander without a destination.

This is one of my favorite day trips from New York City this time of year. Hop on the Metro-North and get off at Philipse Manor Station. From there, it’s about a 10-minute walk to this 19th-century cemetery where writer Washington Irving is buried. After meandering around 90 acres of landscaped grounds, join a special event like an adaptation of Irving’s Bracebridge Hall complete with traditional carols and holiday cheer.

This cemetery was designed to resemble a city (rather than a burial ground) and is world-renowned for its neoclassical gates and beautiful maze of tree-lined paths. There are just under 5,000 burial vaults (all above ground), which include imposing mausoleums made of marble. La Recoleta Cemetery is the final resting place for dozens of Argentine presidents, as well as Nobel laureates and cultural figures.

Located a quick stroll from Hampstead Heath—my most beloved green space in all of London—this legendary cemetery is home to a fascinating mix of cultural figures ranging from Karl Marx to George Eliot (Mary Ann Evans, author of Middlemarch). Travelers can explore both the east and west sides of the cemetery without a guided tour, but why not book one for your first visit to get the full lay of the land? Highgate was modeled after Paris's Père Lachaise Cemetery and now operates as a historic park, nature reserve, and active burial site.

On a peaceful bluff of the Wilmington River, Bonaventure is one of the country’s most gorgeous cemeteries. Live oaks draped in Spanish moss hover above Victorian sculptures and timeworn tombstones belonging to famous figures such as John Muir. (Fun fact: during his thousand-mile walk to the gulf, Muir ran out of money and ended up sleeping in the cemetery, which he later wrote about in a famous chapter titled “Camping Among the Tombs.”)

#6656. Bourbon Caramel Apple Pie

The one thing that can make classic apple pie better? Caramel! That it’s laced with a generous dose of bourbon vaults it straight into hall-of-fame territory. Made using a double batch of our never-fail Perfect Pie Crust, this pretty lattice-topped pie is a crowd-pleaser, familiar enough to appeal to the traditionalists with just enough of a surprise from the booze and the smoky burnt sugar to make the thrill-seekers come back for more. Like all good things, apple pie can’t be rushed. It needs time to chill, bake, and rest—so plan ahead, especially if it’s for Thanksgiving.

Welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

2 hours 15 minutes (plus 7 hours for chilling and cooling)

Whisk 3⅓ cups (417 g) all-purpose flour, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. baking powder in a large bowl to combine. Add 4 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces; rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 1¼ cups (2½ sticks) chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash with your fingers into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea-size).

Make a well in the center of mixture and pour in ½ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute, then knead in bowl a couple of times to bring dough together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn out dough onto a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour; dust top of dough with flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold dough in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting with more flour as needed to prevent sticking. Divide dough in half and pat each piece into a ½"-thick disk. Wrap each disk tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap each disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

Place 1 cup (200 g) granulated sugar and ½ cup water in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot and cover. Bring to a boil over medium heat (no need to stir); cook until sugar is dissolved, 4–7 minutes total. Uncover and continue to cook, stirring or swirling pot occasionally, until caramel turns a deep golden brown, 10–12 minutes.

Add zest of 1 lemon, 3 lb. Honeycrisp apples (about 6 large), peeled, cored, quartered, thinly sliced crosswise, ½ cup bourbon, 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. ground cinnamon to caramel (it may become stiff). Cover and cook, stirring occasionally, until caramel dissolves and apples have released a generous amount of liquid and are tender but still retain their shape (they should look mostly translucent), 15–18 minutes.

Stir ⅓ cup heavy cream, 3 Tbsp. cornstarch, and 2 Tbsp. cool water in a small bowl until cornstarch is dissolved. Pour into apple mixture and cook (it should be bubbling), stirring often, until mixture is thick, about 5 minutes. Transfer filling to a large bowl; let cool. Cover and chill until cold, at least 45 minutes.

Meanwhile, let dough sit at room temperature 5 minutes. Unwrap 1 disk and roll out on a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour to a 12" round, about ¼" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and wrap around rolling pin. Transfer to a 9"-diameter pie pan (such as East Fork Spun Iron Pie Dish). Unfurl into pan, then lift edges and allow dough to slump down into pan. Trim, leaving about a 1" overhang. Chill 15 minutes.

Unwrap remaining disk; roll out on surface lightly dusted with more rice flour to a 18x12" rectangle, about ⅛" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and transfer to a large parchment-lined baking sheet. Brush dough with a thin film of cold water; sprinkle remaining ¼ cup (50 g) granulated sugar over and press gently with your hands to cover dough completely in an even layer (coating dough before cutting into strips will give you the most even coverage). Chill 15 minutes.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 375°. Spoon chilled filling into pie pan and smooth surface to level. Using a ruler, cut dough rectangle into 1"-wide strips. Lay 5–8 strips over filling, spacing evenly across surface to cover. Weave another 5–8 strips over, then under, alternating to create a lattice crust (you may not use all of the strips). Trim overhang to match bottom crust. Press edges of top and bottom crusts firmly together to seal, then trim again, leaving about ¼" overhang. Fold overhang up and over lattice so crust is flush with edges of pan and crimp as desired with lightly floured fingers.

Place pan on a rimmed baking sheet (to catch drips) and bake pie until crust is set and golden, 45–50 minutes. Reduce oven temperature to 350°; continue to bake until crust is deep golden brown and filling is bubbling up through lattice, 40–50 minutes more. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let pie cool in pan at least 4 hours before serving.

Do Ahead: Filling can be made 2 days ahead; keep chilled. Pie can be baked 1 day ahead; store, loosely covered, at room temperature.

#6655. The Clarks Wallabee Goes Gorpcore

Clarks has been on one lately. Over the past few weeks, Moncler worked up the British footwear brand's signature Wallabee, while A.P.C. took on the Desert Boot and the Weaver. Now, Clarks has called in Italian shoemaker Diemme to drag three of its biggest silhouettes up a mountain.

(In case you don't spend all day thinking about Italian hiking boots, here's a primer: Diemme was founded in Montebelluna, a town in northern Italy with a very serious footwear-making history. The brand is best known for taking the kinda boots originally built for mountains and making them nice enough to wear with your very best trousers. Every pair is still made at its factory in Veneto, and the upcoming Clarks collection is, too.)

The main event is the Wallabee, of course. Diemme reworked the familiar moccasin-shaped shoe and covered it in pale “champagne” suede from Charles F. Stead, the British tannery responsible for some of the nicest fuzzy leather in footwear. So far, so classic. But then you get the thick rope laces and rubber mudguard wrapped around the bottom. Underneath, the OG crepe sole has been swapped out for the chunky, lugged unit found on Diemme's Roccia Vet and Cornaro boots. It makes the whole shoe sit higher and gives it enough tread to deal with more than a slightly sticky pub floor. Your ’Bees are now ready to hit the trails.

There are two more styles in the cross-branded collection. The Desert Boot comes in the classic “cola” brown suede, only now it's been fitted with a heavy-duty sole. Then there's the Desert Trek, which has been transformed into a mid-cut boot and made from black full-grain leather. It keeps the signature center seam and little Trek Man logo, but it's easily the biggest and baddest of the three, with metal D-rings running up the lacing system and a beefed up ankle for extra support.

The Diemme x Clarks collection is set to drop on November 5, purchasable through Diemme, Clarks, and select stockists globally.

#6654. Pumpkin Cheesecake Muffins

Loaded with pumpkin seeds, canned pumpkin purée, and pumpkin pie spice, these big streusel-topped muffins are every fall lover’s dream come true. And to make things even better, the inside of each muffin is stuffed with a soft, lightly sweetened cream cheese mixture. Make the cheesecake filling and the streusel ahead of time to pace things out if it’s helpful. Don’t, even for a minute, consider using anything other than Libby’s 100% pure pumpkin purée (not pie mix). Nothing is better. We promise.

This recipe is part of Pumpkin Week 2026, Bon Appétit’s annual celebration of autumn’s most magical pantry staple.

Whisk ⅓ cup coarsely chopped raw pumpkin seeds, ¼ cup (31 g) all-purpose flour, 2 Tbsp. light brown sugar, ½ tsp. pumpkin pie spice, and a pinch of kosher salt in a small bowl to combine. Using your fingers, rub in 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter, room temperature, until moist pea-size lumps form. Chill until ready to use.

Do Ahead: Streusel can be made 1 day ahead. Cover and keep chilled.

Vigorously whisk 6 oz. cream cheese, room temperature, ¼ cup (50 g) granulated sugar, 2 tsp. all-purpose flour, 2 tsp. vanilla extract, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl until combined and smooth.

Do Ahead: Filling can be made 1 day ahead. Cover and chill.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 375°. Line cups of a standard 12-cup muffin pan with paper liners. Whisk 2 large eggs, 1½ cups (packed; 300 g) light brown sugar, 1 cup canned pumpkin purée, ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil, 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, melted, slightly cooled, ¼ cup whole milk, 1 Tbsp. pumpkin pie spice, 1 Tbsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, and 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1 tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl until smooth, about 1 minute. Whisk 1¾ cups (219 g) all-purpose flour and 1½ tsp. baking powder in a small bowl to combine. Add to pumpkin mixture and fold in with a rubber spatula until just incorporated and no large dry streaks of flour remain (don’t overmix; batter will be lumpy).

Bake muffins until streusel is crisp and muffins spring back when gently pressed, 24–27 minutes. Let muffins cool in pan 5 minutes, then turn out onto a wire rack and let cool until just warm or completely.

Do Ahead: Muffins can be made 2 days ahead. Store airtight at room temperature.

#6652. Coperni Closes Following Relationship Breakdown with Distributor

Following months of trying to resolve its conflict with its distributor and shareholder, Tomorrow, Coperni has ceased operations, the brand revealed today.

In a personal memo shared with Vogue Business, co-founders and creative directors Arnaud Vaillant and Sébastien Meyer said they had been unable to fix an ongoing dispute involving unpaid sums.

“These eight years have been extraordinary,” the Coperni duo shared in a personal email. “Coperni has always been a collective adventure, and we are immensely proud of what we have created.” The company thanked the Fédération de la Haute Couture et de la Mode (FHCM), stores, buyers, press, celebrities, models, and other industry figures who had supported them.

“As the world becomes increasingly challenging, particularly in the fashion industry, we believe there is still so much to create and reinvent,” they said. “Innovation has always been our passion and a priority in everything we do. We look ahead with optimism and plenty of ideas, and cannot wait to share them with you.”

In June, Vogue Business reported that Coperni had secured protection from the Paris Court (France’s equivalent of Chapter 11) to help Coperni continue operating. At the time, Vaillant told Vogue Business that the support followed several months of pending payments owed to the brand by Tomorrow, its exclusive distributor and majority shareholder. Additionally, Coperni shared that Tomorrow had terminated its licensing agreement in place.

Complicating the issue, Tomorrow Ltd was sold to Progetto 11 in March. As previously reported, Progetto 11 is the holding company for Italian e-commerce platform The Level Group, which has worked with brands including Palm Angels, Herno, and Off-White. Former CEO and founder of Tomorrow, Stefano Martinetto, stepped down after the sale was completed.

Since then, the Coperni founders had been attempting to buy back their brand from Progretto 11. “Our view is based on what we found when we arrived [at the] end of March: a business already in the middle of a broader dispute about ownership and governance, lacking funding, also resulting in the cancellation of the last fashion show, and founders seeking to reacquire control,” Progetto 11 said in a statement at the time.

In June, Progetto 11 clarified that Coperni has been controlled by two entities: holding company Coperni UK Limited, which holds the license with Tomorrow, and subsidiary Coperni SAS, the main French operating company that oversees day-to-day operations and employs the teams.

Tomorrow acted as a licensor and distributor across its portfolio of brands, receiving all revenues and paying royalties to brands based on their individual deals. Tomorrow would also reimburse brands for costs incurred outside of design — like producing fashion shows or campaigns — but as Tomorrow’s wholesale business faltered due to challenging industry circumstances, Coperni claimed the company ceased paying Coperni’s revenue share and reimbursements.

In fiscal 2024, Tomorrow’s turnover fell 34% to £8.4 million, while gross profit margin decreased from 76% in 2023 to 41% year-on-year. And the company’s operating losses were mounting, up 28% year-on-year to £7.5 million. (Tomorrow had not submitted its fiscal 2025 earnings to Companies House by the time of the sale.)

Tomorrow’s issues first emerged when Coperni abruptly canceled its Fall/Winter 2026 show at Paris Fashion Week. In March, Martine Rose (also in the Tomorrow portfolio) shared a statement noting that she was unable to produce her upcoming collection due to reasons outside her control.

#6651. All About Saoirse Ronan’s Husband, Jack Lowden

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Saoirse Ronan and Jack Lowden have been together for over five years. They tend to keep their lives together very private, but have posted some shots on social media as their relationship progressed.

In July 2024, it was reported that the couple had gotten secretly married. With just a few friends and family members present, they had a ceremony in Edinburgh, Scotland, around the weekend of July 20, 2024. In spring 2025, Ronan revealed her first pregnancy, and the couple was seen pushing a stroller that September.

Here’s everything to know about Lowden and his relationship with Ronan so far.

Lowden is also an actor from Scotland, with a long career onstage. In 2013, he won both an Olivier Award and the Ian Charleson Award for his role as Oswald in Ibsen’s Ghosts. He’s also had some significant roles in film and TV, including Christopher Nolan’s Dunkirk.

In 2020, he bought a home in west Cork with Ronan, but they also live in London and have a terrier named Fran. The couple shares a production company with producer Dominic Norris. Their film The Outrun stars Ronan.

In December 2018, reports surfaced that they were dating after they were seen together at an after-party at Central Park’s Tavern on the Green. The pair played husband and wife in the film Mary Queen of Scots. Sightings of them over the next few years were sparse, and they infrequently appear together on social media. In 2020, they were photographed out in London. In 2022, they were spotted at the Australian Open together. On New Year’s Eve 2023, Lowden shared a mirror selfie of them to celebrate.

In 2019, a reporter for The Telegraph asked Ronan, “Am I allowed to ask if you’re going out with the person that everyone thinks you’re going out with?”

Earlier that year, Lowden was asked about Ronan by ES Magazine and answered the same way, but with more words.

“Oh I’m not going to talk about that. I don’t like talking about that side of life,” he said. “Most of the actors I know live pretty normal lives, it’s just every now and again they have to do something ridiculous or extraordinary. My life hasn’t changed. People seem more interested—I guess that’s changed, for sure.”

Lowden has gushed about Ronan when talking about her acting, including in an interview with i newspaper.

“The woman is a force of nature, on- and offscreen, and utterly fearless and a brilliant leader as well,” he said. “My first love is actors, and when you’re given a Ferrari like her, it’s all about how you make everything good for the Ferrari to show off. Don’t make a Ferrari do what a Renault Clio does. It’s a dreadful analogy, but they’re like gold dust, good actors. When there’s someone like that, you just have to facilitate them and you will get gold. And my God, did we.”

He praised her again in a March 2025 interview with The Times, saying that seeing her perform in Mary Queen of Scots inspired him to keep acting and not quit. “There was me at 27 thinking about stopping because I felt self-conscious or like I didn’t know how to do it,” he said. “And then watching this 23-year-old carry the weight of a huge film like that with ease and grace and majesty. It was remarkable to watch. She makes it look so easy, like breathing. It was totally inspiring.”

The pair made their debut on the carpet as a married couple at the 76th Primetime Emmy Awards at the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles on Sept. 15, 2024. Lowden wore a classic black tux with satin lapels. Ronan was wearing a custom Louis Vuitton two-piece with a sleeveless top and trailing skirt. Around her neck, she wore a stunning diamond necklace by Bulgari.

In an October 2024 interview with USA Today, Ronan shared that she once thought she’d “never” have a partner or a “beautiful network” of people because her career kept her so busy.

“My life has become so much more than just work,” Ronan said. “For a long time, that’s all I did; that’s how I met people and made sense of the world.”

She continued, “I feel like I’m part of a group, which I never thought I would have. I used to think, ‘You’ll never have friends. You’ll never have a partner.’ I was so in my own world, in a lot of ways. So now, to feel like I’ve got a very rich personal and social life—it’s so precious to me.”

In March 2025, Lowden offered rare comments on his relationship with Ronan in his The Times interview. When asked how they keep their marriage strong as two actors whose jobs sometimes require travel, he said, “[We] just have to check in with each other a lot. Obviously it made it a lot easier when we worked on the same project.”

They plan to work together again, he added, “but the question is, how do we do it, because Saoirse, she has ambitions as well to direct.”

On May 22, 2025, Ronan made an appearance at the Louis Vuitton Cruise at Palais des Papes in Avignon, France, wearing a semi-sheer dress by the fashion house that revealed she and Lowden are expecting their first child. The silky black gown was covered in matching black lace trim and folded around her body, showing off her black sandals under the asymmetrical skirt.

On May 31, the couple was seen in London. Ronan wore a form-fitting black bodysuit that appeared to show off her pregnant figure, under a puffer jacket and a sweater tied around her waist. She had on a baseball cap and sunglasses. Lowden was dressed in black sweatpants and an Adidas hoodie and was carrying a backpack.

On Sept. 11, 2025, Hello! reported that the couple had quietly welcomed their first baby. According to the outlet, Ronan and Lowden were seen earlier this month in London pushing a stroller. Lowden later spoke about becoming a father in his November 2026 GQ cover story.

Speaking to People, Ronan revealed that she hopes to act alongside her husband in the future. “I mean, I would love for us to work together again. I’ve said to him I really want him to do a play with me because he’s so incredible onstage, and that’s where he really comes to life,” she said.

“I think that’s where he feels at his best, and it’s not necessarily where I feel at my best, so I would really like to do it with him so he can hold my hand a little bit,” Ronan continued. “I mean, listen, we met through work and we’ve produced stuff together, and we’re very much a part of one another’s work life as well as personal life.”

Still, Ronan said Lowden needs a little more convincing. “It just feels like when the right thing comes along, it would be the obvious choice for us to do it together. But I think he’s more hesitant to work with me than I am with him,” she said. “I don’t know. I think he just finds it weird. He finds it weird working with any of his friends. He gets embarrassed.”

Lowden praised his wife’s acting and opened up about being a father for the first time in his GQ profile.

He reflected on watching her shoot a film in Italy that summer. “I’m going to sound a bit soppy, but getting to watch her act, in the flesh—that’s how we met—is really wonderful,” he said. “She’s so at home doing it.”

He also spoke about welcoming their first child in 2025. “Since I was a kid, I always knew I wanted to be a dad, and now I am,” he admitted. “You become aware that you’ll watch your kid grow up—sounds morbid—and you think, ‘Oh my God, I’m in charge of a kid, and I’m still a kid myself.’”

#6650. Salted Coffee Custard Pie

If you can’t be fussed with making coffee and dessert after a big holiday dinner, consider this twofer instead. The silky, sliceable, cool custard is rich and intense with two kinds of coffee, while the oatmeal crust is a tweedy-textured study in contrast. It’s prebaked to mitigate sogginess but doesn’t require pie weights. Mascarpone keeps the whipped cream firm and fluffy for a full 24 hours.

Don’t be tempted to skip the cold-brew concentrate. You don’t want regular cold brew, and definitely not brewed and cooled coffee from your coffee machine at home, no matter how fancy. The concentrate (highly recommend Grady’s Cold Brew Coffee Concentrate) is consistent every single time with exactly the right strength to stand up to the dairy and eggs in the filling.

Cook’s notes: This pie requires a 9"-diameter deep-dish pie dish.

Welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

Place a rack in middle of oven and preheat to 350°. Butter pie dish with unsalted butter. Pulse 2 cups (180 g) old-fashioned oats, ¼ cup (31 g) all-purpose flour, ¼ cup (packed; 50 g) dark brown sugar, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a food processor until oats are coarsely ground. Drizzle in 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter, melted, slightly cooled; pulse just until mixture comes together. Transfer to prepared dish (such as East Fork Ceramic Pie Plate); wipe out and reserve food processor. Press crust firmly and evenly across bottom and up sides of dish with a flat-bottomed measuring cup. Bake until golden and surface looks dry, 25–30 minutes. Transfer crust to a wire rack; reduce oven temperature to 325°.

Pulse 1 cup (packed; 200 g) dark brown sugar, 2 Tbsp. all-purpose flour, 2 Tbsp. instant espresso powder, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in food processor until no lumps remain, about 1 minute. Add 3 large eggs, ½ cup (1 stick) unsalted butter, melted, slightly cooled, and 1 Tbsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract and pulse until smooth. Add 1 cup cold-brew coffee concentrate and 2 cups heavy cream and pulse until well combined.

Pour custard into crust (it’s okay if crust is still warm). Bake pie until edges of filling are set and slightly puffed but center still wobbles a little when gently shaken, 40–50 minutes (filling will continue to set after baking). Transfer to a wire rack; let cool at least 3 hours, or, preferably, chill 12 hours.

Using an electric mixer, beat ½ cup mascarpone, 4 Tbsp. granulated sugar, remaining 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, ⅔ cup heavy cream, and 1 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract in a medium bowl until soft peaks form. Spoon whipped cream mixture over pie; swirl lightly to create divots and peaks.

Just before serving, dust with instant espresso powder if desired; sprinkle generously with flaky sea salt.

Do ahead: Pie (without espresso powder and sea salt garnishes) can be made 1 day ahead. Cover loosely and keep chilled.

#6649. The Best Early Black Friday Clothing Deals 2026 Are Here

Before you start questioning your own reality, Black Friday is still a ways away. But it's not too early to start taking advantage of some early Black Friday clothing deals that already sprouting up. Retailers seem more eager than ever to get the sales started early this year, and at this rate, Black Friday will be here before you know it. And some of the hardest-hitting discounts land before the official day even kicks off.

And it’s not just like the stalwarts like Gap, Banana Republic, Abercrombie and J.Crew in the mix, although they are heavily in the mix. Killer indies like Lost & Found and Haven also have a host of discounted goods, and outdoor behemoth REI is feeling especially generous for early November. So, if you’re trying to shop away the daylight savings blues or just feel like getting a jump on holiday shopping, you’re in the right spot.

Abercrombie doesn’t have any specific promotions that are live at the moment, but the sale section was recently stuffed with some ideal fall building blocks—most notably some baggy cords—that will make a refresh as easy and affordable as you’d ever hoped it could be.

Banana Republic has been on a heater recently, and the perfectly-curated Archive Reissue collection is leading the charge this season. It should also be noted that anything on the site that is on sale also gets an additional 20% off.

Don’t tell anyone at Gap that Black Friday is a ways off, because there are a ridiculous number of in-season pieces up to 50%—sweaters, flannels, cords, jeans, jackets, and more—and it feels like raising too much awareness to that might cause some reconsideration and none of us want that.

Haven isn’t promoting a sale anywhere on the site and you might have to dig a little bit depending what size you wear, but if you’re looking for some of the sickest IYKYK brands on the planet at insane discounts, there aren’t many places I’d rather start.

If you’re not familiar with Huckberry, they preside over one of most thoughtfully curated assortments of menswear, footwear and gear anywhere, whether that’s IRL or URL. They haven’t kicked off anything Black Friday specific yet—again, it’s early—but if you haven’t gone through the sale tab in a while, you’re missing out on some preposterously good deals.

Nearly all of J.Crew’s spring-summer collection is on sale at the moment, over 300 pieces up to 40% off through May 26—including a whole bunch of heat-beating shirting, lightweight pants, archive classics and basically anything else you’d want to be on sale.

The first name in denim has a pretty nifty “buy two, get 30% off” promotion going on site-wide, so if you’re searching for some jeans, you might just want to buy a couple pairs. (Or maybe a trucker. Or sherpa-lined trucker. You’re in charge.)

Diving into Lost & Found’s sale section is one of the more enjoyable shopping experiences one can have online right now: the selection is great, the brand list is a top-five worldwide and there’s plenty of inventory, which puts it in stark contrast with some of the less rewarding sale sections.

One of the most quietly great, easy-to-wear brands in the game recently reloaded the sale section, and basically no category was left unturned. Of particular note, are the killer sweatshirts currently available with a healthy discount applied.

Mr Porter’s sale section is the kind you can lose an hour in without realizing it, even months after a seasonal sale has ended. Case in point: there’s roughly 500 pairs of shoes and 900 jackets on sale at this very moment, and while sizes might be hit and miss, the deals aren’t.

REI’s Deals section always lives up to the billing, but right now it’s about as good as it’s ever been. Hundreds of pieces from heavyweights like Arc’teryx, Patagonia, The North Face and more are discounted up to 50%, including plenty of winter-specific gear for anyone lacking in that department.

Todd Snyder presumably won’t be partaking in the Black Friday festivities this year—they announced a new sale structure a while back—but that doesn’t mean the already-on-sale fare doesn’t hold up to the promotions sure to fire up across the board.

This year in the US, Black Friday is on Friday, November 27, a day after Thanksgiving. While that’s the official date, many retailers roll out deals throughout November. You can expect the biggest discounts to happen between Thanksgiving and Cyber Monday, but be on the look out for retailers to launch sales early.

Cyber Monday lands on November 30 this year, the Monday after Thanksgiving. Most brands keep the deals rolling through the week—but that doesn't mean a deal will last all day, so act fast.

Are clothing deals better on Black Friday or Cyber Monday?

Black Friday and Cyber Monday both deliver a plethora of clothing deals, but they play a little differently. Big-name retailers and legacy brands usually kick things off on Black Friday, while smaller menswear boutiques tend to hold their fire until Cyber Monday. Expect solid discounts starting around 20% off—and keep your eyes peeled for the coveted sale-on-sale action that’s become the norm in recent years.

#6648. Nathan Fielder’s Elizabeth Holmes Documentary, You Can See Everything: What We Know So Far

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Elizabeth Holmes’s story is getting told in a new project with Nathan Fielder at the helm. The comedian has released his new documentary titled You Can See Everything about Holmes, founder of the now-defunct biotech company Theranos, before she began serving her 11-year prison sentence for committing fraud.

Unlike a typical documentary, the film features Fielder chatting with Holmes in a Q&A format, while an unnamed A-list actress reenacts the events of the documentary in asides as Holmes. Here’s everything we know about You Can See Everything.

The official logline for the documentary reads: “34 days before she’s sent to prison, notorious Silicon Valley founder Elizabeth Holmes invites a skeptical film crew to document her every move. What begins as an intimate portrait of an enigmatic felon becomes a mind-bending three-year journey into the abyss. From boundary-pushing directors Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim comes You Can See Everything.”

Audiences were buzzing at Telluride Film Festival, where the doc premiered with a surprise screening on September 6. Variety called the doc “a shameless, fascinating, reality-TV-eats-its-tail look at entitled duplicity” and said “the sensation of ‘WTF? I’ve got to watch this!’ did not subside as the movie went on. It only intensified.”

Deadline reported that “the nearly three-hour-long film drew continuous laughter, frequently triggered by hilarious reaction shots of Fielder...attempting to process what Holmes and Evans [Holmes’s partner] are pushing.” And the L.A. Times said the movie contains “mind-bending twists that meld reality and performance.”

The documentary is currently available to watch in theaters, but it will likely hit HBO Max when it comes to streaming. Warner Bros. Discovery owns HBO and HBO Max, and the company has an agreement that states A24 titles will automatically go to HBO Max as their first stop on streaming after the theatrical window and PVOD (Premium Video on Demand) release windows are over. You Can See Everything currently has no streaming release date.

In addition to Fielder and Holmes, The Hollywood Reporter confirmed that an unnamed “A-list actress” has a role in the making of the documentary. Her identity has not been revealed, as “the filmmakers and fest [Telluride Film Festival] requested that her identity be kept secret until more people have a chance to see the movie.”

As for what viewers can expect from the A-list actress, THR reports her cameo is “the craziest twist of a crazy film,” but her involvement is accidental. After agreeing to meet with Fielder, she finds herself wanting to be involved in the filming process and “winds up becoming a full-fledged collaborator in the film, appearing throughout the rest of it alternatingly as herself, giving commentary on the insanity of the situation, and then in reenactments—long Fielder’s go-to way of making sense of things—as Holmes.”

The first official trailer for the documentary arrived on September 8, featuring Fielder and Holmes having an unsettling conversation.

“I don’t have anything to deceive you on. Of course I’m not deceiving you. I’m engaging with you as a human being. Why would I deceive you? There’s no...there’s no reason for me to do that,” Holmes tells Fielder.

“You’re being real right now?” he asks her, to which Holmes replies, “I’m always being real.”

A first-look image was also released with the trailer, which shows Holmes preparing to give an item to a child, while Fielder looks at her from the background.

The first official trailer arrived on September 23 and provides a close look into some of the conversations that Fielder and Holmes had with each other throughout the film.

“You really feel you did nothing wrong?” Fielder asks her, to which Holmes replies, “I did not.”

He presses her and follows up the question with, “So where did things get lost? How are you where you are right now?”

Holmes finds herself at a loss: “I wish I knew. I don’t know. I don’t feel like I understand that,” she tells him.

At another point in the trailer, Fielder questions how Holmes could be so calm about his filming her every move. When he asks Holmes if she has any “worry” about him being at her home 24/7, she answers, “I don’t think so. I think this is the moment in time to capture this story before I’m gone.”

The comedian also manages to interview Holmes’s partner, William “Billy” Evans, who reveals he fell in love with her in their first conversation. “Weren’t you worried she was scamming you?” Fielder asks.

Evans coolly responds, “100 percent, but what does she has to gain from me?”

When Fielder reminds him that his family is wealthy—Evans is the heir to the Evans Hotel Group—he responds, “I think there’s a lot of different levels of wealth.”

Neither Holmes nor Evans have seen the doc, Oppenheim revealed during an October Q&A after the film’s Los Angeles screening. “Neither of them have seen the film. Elizabeth is still incarcerated; Billy hasn’t seen it,” the director said, with The Hollywood Reporter adding that Evans has “a strained relationship with the crew.”

Fielder added that Evans “started trying to exert a level of control over the process that made it very hard to engage with him, and it was uncomfortable for us and also A24 and everyone. And I think we sort of had to stop—I think communication broke down basically, and we’ve been in that like state for a little bit. So it’s been challenging in that way.”

On November 2, Evans revealed the “one misconception” about his relationship with Holmes following the release of the movie. “That I somehow control Liz. Anyone who actually knows her would find that idea hilarious,” he responded to an X user.

Evans added, “She’s fiercely independent, strong willed, and my best friend. We are partners in every sense. We challenge each other, disagree, and face the world together. Her closest friends are also some of my closest friends. If I ever mistreated her, they’d have my head.”

Yes. In 2019, HBO released The Inventor: Out for Blood in Silicon Valley, which explored the rise and fall of Holmes and her multibillion-dollar company, Theranos.

In 2022, The Dropout—also about the rise and fall of Holmes and Theranos—premiered on Hulu. Amanda Seyfried starred as Holmes in the miniseries.
