#6643. Farmers Market Salad With Miso Maple Dressing

Most recipes serve multiple people. In Me, Myself, and Dinner, each dish serves one and only one. That's you! Because whether you live solo (almost 30% of Americans do) or are enjoying a night to yourself, sitting down to a meal should be something to look forward to.

The farmers market is my biggest hack for solo cooking. Instead of committing to a three-pound bag of carrots, you can buy just one, and choose your produce based on beauty or mere curiosity. That’s how I came up with this fall salad, comprising a single head of Little Gem lettuce and some crunchy produce, including that carrot we mentioned, cucumber, watermelon radish, and an Asian pear. Slicing those elements thinly with a mandoline and throwing them in an ice bath for a brief soak helps keep everything cold and crisp.

The dressing is equally important. I start with Kewpie mayo for its richness and savory depth—it’s made with only egg yolks and contains MSG, giving it a fuller flavor than standard mayonnaise. White miso brings even more umami, while rice vinegar keeps things bright. The result is a creamy finger-licking dressing that clings to every bite. Serve with a fried egg (or your protein of choice) and a piece of fresh bread to scoop up the leftovers. Make a double batch of dressing for dipping crudités or marinating salmon, chicken, or roasted vegetables.

Read More: The Farmers Market Is Built for Solo Cooking

Combine 1 small head of Little Gem or other crunchy lettuce, leaves separated, cut into 2"–3" pieces, 1 rainbow carrot, peeled, very thinly sliced lengthwise into ribbons with a mandoline or vegetable peeler, 1 Persian cucumber, thinly sliced, preferably with a mandoline, ½ small watermelon radish, peeled, halved, thinly sliced into half-moons, preferably with a mandoline, and ¼ medium Asian pear, thinly sliced into half-moons, preferably with a mandoline, in a large bowl of ice water. Let soak 10–15 minutes.

Meanwhile, whisk ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil, 2 Tbsp. seasoned rice vinegar, 2 Tbsp. white miso, 2 tsp. Kewpie mayonnaise, 2 tsp. pure maple syrup, and 1 tsp. toasted sesame oil in a small bowl until smooth and emulsified (or combine in a small glass jar, cover, and shake). Taste dressing and season with kosher salt.

Drain vegetables and run through a salad spinner or pat dry with a kitchen towel to remove excess water. Wipe out large bowl, return vegetables to bowl, and drizzle 2 Tbsp. dressing over. Toss, adding more dressing as needed, until evenly coated (reserve any remaining dressing for another use).

Transfer salad to a shallow bowl or rimmed plate. Top with a fried egg and serve with country-style bread if desired.

Do Ahead: Dressing can be made up to 3 days ahead. Cover and chill.

#6642. Who Is Elizabeth Holmes’s Partner, Billy Evans?

This story contains spoilers for You Can See Everything.

When Nathan Fielder asked Elizabeth Holmes to document the days leading up to her serving her prison sentence for his new A24 documentary, You Can See Everything, the proposition meant that he would also be spending a large portion of the shoot with Holmes’s partner, Billy Evans.

The documentary spends time delving into Holmes’s public legal scandal with Theranos—the now-defunct biotech company that saw her committing investment fraud—but it also sheds light on Holmes and Evans’s relationship and how they have managed to thrive despite her sentencing.

As the documentary, co-directed by Lance Oppenheim, progresses, Fielder’s focus shifts from Holmes to Evans. “Weren’t you worried she was scamming you?” Fielder asked him at one point, to which Evans responded, “100 percent, but what does she have to gain from me?” When presented with the knowledge of his family’s wealth, Evans defended Holmes and said, “I think there’s a lot of different levels of wealth.” Things only snowball from there.

Evans’s grandparents, William and Anne Evans, own the Evans Hotel Group. Founded in 1953, Evans Hotels consists of three luxury properties, which include The Lodge Terry Pines, the Bahia Resort Hotel, and the Catamaran Resort Hotel and Spa. All three of the properties are located in California.

Evans’s LinkedIn profile revealed that he attended the Massachusetts Institute of Technology between 2011 and 2015. He earned his bachelor’s degree in economics.

Evans’s LinkedIn also revealed that he’s the CEO of Haemanthus, his self-founded AI-driven medical testing startup; he’s held the role since 2022. The company aims to achieve a mission similar to that of Holmes’s Theranos, which sought to provide blood diagnostics through one drop of blood with the Edison machine. Instead of using one drop of blood for diagnostics, Haemanthus is working to create a device that tests blood in addition to urine and saliva for the presence of diseases.

“This is not Theranos 2.0. Theranos attempted to miniaturize existing tests. Our approach is fundamentally different. We use light to read the complete molecular story in biological fluids, seeing patterns current tests can’t detect. Not an improvement. A different paradigm,” the company shared in a statement to Fortune in 2025, following reports of Holmes advising on the project. “Setting the record straight. Elizabeth Holmes has zero involvement in Haemanthus. We’ve learned from her company’s mistakes, but she has no role, now or future.”

In a 2023 joint interview with The New York Times, Evans revealed that he and Holmes fell for each other fast. “To say we immediately fell in love isn’t an overstatement,” he said.

Holmes, however, noted that Evans had some reservations about entering a relationship with her. “It had been two years of all this stuff written about me, and I think you get to know someone in a totally different way when you walk in with that skepticism versus if you meet when everything is sunshine and roses,” she said. “That allowed us to get to know each other in a really deep way.” The couple got engaged in August 2018.

Holmes gave birth to their son, William Holmes Evans, in 2021. By 2023, a court document revealed that Holmes gave birth to her and Evans’s second child, a daughter named Invicta.

Evans attended several of Holmes’s court dates, appearing by her side on the way to and from her hearings. In January 2022, she was found guilty of three counts of wire fraud and one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud. She’s currently serving her sentence—which was reduced to nine years from 11 years—at Federal Prison Camp Bryan in Texas. She will be transferred to a halfway house in August 2027.

While Holmes was sentenced, Evans asked the court in November 2022 to shorten her sentence so she could enjoy more special moments with their son. “My heart is broken with the thought of spending any days away from Liz, for a future in which my son grows up with a relationship with his mother on the other side of glass armed by guards,” he said. Evans still visits Holmes regularly, with him telling People in February 2025 that it has been “hell and torture” at the prison facility. The tech CEO added that it “shatters” Holmes when she says goodbye to him and her family.

You Can See Everything makes some shocking revelations about Evans, like that he posts from Holmes’s X account while she’s in prison (for a while, it was without her knowledge), and that he arranged to be paid for his and Holmes’s appearance in the documentary, which he ultimately rescinded. (It’s unclear whether Holmes knew about the deal.)

During a screening of the film in L.A. this month, Fielder said of the couple, “Neither of them have seen the film. Elizabeth is still incarcerated; Billy hasn’t seen it.” He added, according to The Hollywood Reporter, that Evans “started trying to exert a level of control over the process that made it very hard to engage with him, and it was uncomfortable for us and also A24 and everyone. And I think we sort of had to stop—I think communication broke down basically, and we’ve been in that like state for a little bit. So it’s been challenging in that way.”

Evans confirmed that he hasn’t seen the film during an interview with the All In podcast, which was released on October 15. “I haven’t seen it. I might think this is the dumbest thing I have ever done,” Evans said, per Variety. He has seen the trailer and said that Holmes “looks insane” in it. Evans added, “Am I nervous? I have been through so many intense, surreal experiences that it takes a bit to raise my blood pressure. With this, there’s certainly concern, but it’s ultimately our decision.”

On November 3, Evans revealed the “one misconception” about his relationship with Holmes following the release of the movie: “That I somehow control Liz. Anyone who actually knows her would find that idea hilarious,” he responded to an X user.

Evans added, “She’s fiercely independent, strong willed, and my best friend. We are partners in every sense. We challenge each other, disagree, and face the world together. Her closest friends are also some of my closest friends. If I ever mistreated her, they’d have my head.”

In a separate tweet, Evans revealed that he misses “everything about [Holmes].” He wrote, “I miss her presence. Her touch. The way she runs her fingers through my hair. Her patience. She makes me a better person. And without her, I feel an emptiness that’s hard to describe. People often say they need someone when what they really mean is that they want them. I’ve thought a lot about that distinction. I need Liz. She should qualify as a medically necessary prescription.”

On All In, Evans elaborated on why he wanted to make the film ahead of Holmes’s 11-year sentence. “She’s been prevented from speaking publicly in any way, shape, or form, and this would come out after that period in which she is now allowed to talk,” he said. “There’s been a lot of media produced on her. There’s been a lot of people who have told her story. That narrative is pretty ossified. The whole idea was: Here she is, see her and make up your own mind. It’s not to re-litigate the case. Practically, at this time she was not allowed to talk about the case, so she was gonna follow the rules and not talk about the case.”

He explained that his own loved ones have thought he was “crazy” for knowing—and now being in a relationship with—Holmes. “And they would meet her and spend time with her and see her in a totally natural environment, like going on a hike or helping a friend. Every opinion of her would radically shift,” Evans said. “That was the intention of the film. To help scale that up and allow other people to sit with her and make up their own minds.”

#6641. The 9 Best Hotels in Vermont for the Perfect New England Getaway

Known for its picturesque little towns and scenic mountain views (and, equally importantly, its cheese), Vermont is worth a visit year-round—but it really comes alive in the fall, when the foliage is at its peak and the brisk chill in the air is still a novelty. From charming towns like Woodstock to lakeside cities like Burlington and outdoorsy havens like Stowe, the New England state doesn’t disappoint if you’re traveling in search of autumnal activities. And just like their surroundings, the best hotels in Vermont are full of charm.

Travelers looking for sleek accommodation with glitzy furnishings should probably go elsewhere: this is the time to lean into the rustic appeal of the region. Quaint bed and breakfasts, cozy inns, and inviting lodges are the way to go—so with this in mind, we pulled nine options from across the state. Cue the cider.

I recently spent a fall weekend at the Seminary, at a time when the surrounding foliage was in peak form and the brisk air made certain features—like an antique claw-foot tub and wood-burning fireplace—especially appealing. Each guest room has its own personality, outfitted with original artwork and vintage furniture (made modern with touches like Bellino Italian bedding and chrome desk lamps). There’s a cranberry-colored room with a matching velvet seating area; a moody blue room with a gorgeous antique room divider; a cozy little mauve room with ornate wooden furniture and marbled lampshades where I made myself at home. The real highlight, though, is the communal space. It’s hard to pick a favorite between the aqua blue kitchen, complete with a raspberry-colored zellige backsplash that could inspire even the most cooking-averse to whip up pancakes, and the colorful living room where sunlight streams through oversized windows; either way, this is a spot that encourages gathering the whole friend group together for a weekend away.

This 53-room Alpine-inspired spot is lodge living at its finest. Explorers book it for its prime location directly on Cady Hill Forest, which has multiple trails for hiking and biking. Spend your rest day alternating between the hot tub, sauna, and its two pools. The design leans rustic (give or take a couple of Togo chairs), with moss green paneling, tartan upholstery, and wood beams running throughout. It’s all centered around a Great Room, a multi-use space that houses both daily breakfast and a bar—the ideal spot to unwind by the fire after a day outdoors.

If you’ve ever wondered what a woodsy cabin would look like with a Wabi-Sabi-inspired overhaul, AWOL is the answer. The 35-room boutique hotel pulls inspiration from organic shapes and washed-out color palettes, resulting in a deeply tranquil space. If you’re visiting in the winter to take advantage of the nearby slopes, make sure to book a room that comes with ski racks—and bring a swimsuit for a dip in the cedar hot tub while you’re at it. (Your sore muscles will thank you after.) The complimentary breakfast, which is served daily in the light-filled lodge space, is another highlight. (It features an artisanal toast bar, which is frankly too intriguing to pass up.)

For a city stay that still feels tucked away, book a room at Blind Tiger. Originally a mansion built in 1881, the 14-room boutique hotel feels like staying at your eccentric friend’s country home in the best way; splashy decor and mixed prints characterize the aesthetic, and many of the pieces are handmade or one-of-a-kind. (Plus, as none of the rooms come with a TV, unplugging is heavily encouraged.) The central solarium is a great place to unwind with a book and a cup of tea in the afternoons, too.

Another Bluebird by Lark project (this one predating the Cady Hill Lodge by two years), Tälta Lodge offers itself up as a slightly more pared-back alternative. There are 51 rooms and suites, many of which come with balconies for soaking up the great outdoors. That’s not to say it skimps on amenities: the indoor pool is heated, and the bar lobby is stocked with local beer on tap.

Dating back to 1793, it’ll be hard to find a more historic stay in Vermont than the 142-room Woodstock Inn & Resort. The sprawling property has been updated many times—most recently in 2018—and today includes all the luxurious bells and whistles without sacrificing that old-school charm. Dine at one of the on-site restaurants for those days when it’s too cold to venture out; Richardson’s Tavern focuses on locally sourced ingredients with a contemporary twist, like a chanterelle-and-cherry tomato bucatini pasta or crispy quail served with pickled blackberries and poultry jus.

The very picture of a quaint New England B&B, this place has a small number of guest rooms that put on a charm offensive: some have working fireplaces, others have mountain views, and all have a distinctly old-school inn feel. In addition to a full country breakfast served daily in the dining room, the property includes a French-Vermont fine dining restaurant to book if you’re traveling to celebrate a special occasion.

Sitting on 112 acres of lush land that includes everything from a trout pond to apple orchards, this hotel has no shortage of activities (including pastry classes and archery lessons, if you need a break from all the hiking and biking and want to stay put for a day). In terms of accommodation, you have a similarly vast number of options. Stay in a Historic Inn room for farmhouse simplicity, a Coldbrook room for a more pampered experience, or the Carriage House for a group trip.

For a true country inn experience, stay at the Rabbit Hill. No two suites are remotely alike: in one, you’ll find a rustic cedar four-poster bed set against tartan wallpaper, while in the next room over, a California-inspired, honey-colored design scheme awaits. Start your day off with the free breakfast, pop in for afternoon tea, and end the night with marshmallow roasting at the fire pit or a martini in the British-inspired pub. When you’re not snacking, book an ATV tour of the country roads or try your hand at canoeing—the hotel can help you set up a host of activities, so you’ll never be bored.

#6640. WNBA Finals MVP Gabby Williams on Game 7, Trans Athletes, and Her Cat, Halle Berry

“Print this,” said Joe Lacob, the billionaire owner of the Golden State Valkyries, at the start of the team’s playoff run. “Gabby Williams is the best player in the world."

It was one of the coldest quotes in recent sports memory. But at the time, Williams, the 30-year-old French-American wing, hadn’t yet won a WNBA Championship, much less been named Finals MVP. And, truth be told, no one expected this from the Valkyries, an expansion franchise in only its second year of existence, and one without a single All-WNBA selection on its roster.

No matter. After defeating the Atlanta Dream in a winner-takes-all Game 7 (the first in WNBA history) this past weekend, the Valkyries brought their first ever WNBA Trophy back to the Bay. And it was largely because of Williams, who lived up to Lacob’s promise by executing the most memorable second-half takeover in WNBA Finals history.

Here’s how it went down: With three minutes left in the third, the Valks trailing by six, Williams called for the ball, went between-the-legs, and took a step back jumper from beyond the perimeter. She followed that up moments later with a catch-and-shoot three in Angel Reese’s grill. The following possession, Williams freed herself up from a double team, then sprinted out past the three-point line for a money ball.

Williams’ back-to-back-to-back triples broke Atlanta and gave life to “Ballhalla,” San Francisco’s fortress of 18,064 violet-clad, women’s basketball fanatics. After trailing for most of the game, Golden State snatched the lead and didn’t look back. Williams finished with 28 points in the second half (a WNBA post-season record) on her way to a game-high 30. When it came time to name the Finals MVP, there was little question about which player on an otherwise balanced roster had been most crucial to the Valkyries’ fairytale fun.

Watching Williams, you might not have guessed that, when she’s not hooping, she simply wants to cuddle with her cat and binge-watch anime. Just before the Valks’ championship parade, GQ got to know this smooth assassin a bit more intimately.

No matter what, when I was overseas, as soon as I came home, I would tell HB how my game went. It's the first thing I do. I walk in the door, “Oh, HB, we lost today. I played so bad.” Or “Oh, HB, we won. And this happened.” First thing I do [after winning the WNBA Finals], “HB, we freaking won. Can you believe it?” And she was like, “Can you feed me?”

I love animals, and I do have two family dogs who I absolutely love. But a cat is just like, they have boundaries. Dogs are kind of dumb and just they'll love whoever walks in the door. Once you earn a cat's love, there's no better feeling than that. I'll want to cuddle with HB and she's like, “No, not now.” But when she wants to cuddle, it's like, Oh. And she's definitely a Velcro cat. She sleeps right here [next to my face] and there's just no better feeling.

The coaches knew that Atlanta had been putting a lot of tension on me defensively all series and it was causing me to… It was really tough to find my rhythm. So Nat [head coach Natalie Nakase] was just like, “Let the game come to you. Stay patient. The game will open up.” She's like, “Just wait till the game opens up.” At Halftime, V [Veronica Burton] looked at me, she was like, “What do you need?” And I was like, “I'm good. I'm going to get going. I got it.” She's like, “Okay, I got you.” So V was a really big one in helping me out of that locker room because she just looked at me just like, “I trust you.” And that was huge just to see that in her eyes. And then [assistant coach] Sugar Rodgers, who I've leaned on all season, she was like, “Go off.”

She's like, “I'm waiting for you to go off.” And I was like, “I got you.” KP [assistant coach Kasib Powell] and [assistant coach] Landon [Tatum], both of them were like, “We got the first play for you. Get going, open it up, and the rest is yours." Having that trust after seeing how that first half went and everyone just going like, even with 20 minutes left in the last game of our season, that's not as much of a testament to me, but a testament to the trust that we have as a team.

When I hit that shot, I wasn't thinking about it in the game, but as soon as I hit it and I heard the crowd pop, I was like, “Yeah, they've been waiting for this.” I could tell that the fans were like, “Finally, Gabby. Dang.” But in the most positive way ever. So I saw one go through, and I didn't realize until I came home hours after the game, and then I finally opened social media after the party and stuff, and I was like, “Oh, those three’s were three possessions in a row.” I didn't realize that in the moment.

I've been in deficits before where you come back and all you can think about is stop, score, stop, score. You're not thinking about what happened in the last possession. So I swear, I didn't realize that it was literally three possessions in a row until I came home and watched something I was tagged in. And I was like, “That's kind of crazy.”

I love how he's just so aloof. I think that's what everyone loves about him. My partner has never seen Attack on Titan. I'm like, “There's no way.” So we're actually watching all of it. Well, I'm rewatching it. She's watching it for the first time. I'm like, “This is exactly the show I need to be watching right now during this final series.” So yeah, I channeled Levi. The night before the Finals game, she just started season three, and it's the scene when you first see Kenny [the Ripper] and the famous [scene of Levi] yelling “Kenny” [in battle]. I felt like I needed that.

It's so fulfilling to play for something so much bigger than yourself. I think it's very easy as an athlete to get caught up in personal accolades, check boxes in your career. But I mean, I can compare it to the national team where there’s just a whole different kind of pressure that I love when you're putting a country on your shoulders.

I could feel that here where I'm like, I don't want to let this community down. And seeing that these fans show up from our first game of preseason before anyone knew we would be good, or maybe they did. I didn't want to let them down. I wanted them to celebrate. I wanted my AAU coach to freaking celebrate. I want him to say that he has an ex-player who's a champion. My family, they've been taking flights back and forth to Atlanta, to Vegas. They've been driving up from Reno every day, and I'm like, I want to give this back to them for doing all of this for me.

And obviously, I’m part of the queer community. Of course, I’m very close to a lot of trans people, and they’re humans. We’re all just human, whether you agree with me or not.

At the end of the day, we all just deserve to have a chance. So it's a no-brainer. I just speak my mind. I speak how I feel. I'm not going to try to be, I guess, media-trained. If I'm saying something and it pisses you off and you want me to compromise my character so you can consume my media better, don't consume anything. Don't watch me play. If it bothers you that much that I care about human lives or whatever it is, that's fine. If I pissed off a bigot, great.

#6639. The Best Teriyaki in Seattle

Who serves the best gorditas in Mexico City? Or Baltimore's can't-miss crab cakes? Welcome to Taste of the Town, where we call on a local expert to share the best versions of one of their city’s most iconic foods. Here, we explore Seattle’s take on teriyaki.

Seattle’s entire teriyaki universe exists because of one man, a pioneer of chargrilled chicken thighs. In 1976, Toshi Kasahara opened a restaurant serving lightly marinated and grilled chicken, glazed in a blend of soy sauce, ginger, garlic, and sugar. This wasn’t any teriyaki you’d find in Japan, but a cheap, filling, flavor-packed translation aimed at a working-class city still unaware of the tech boom on the horizon.

Kasahara established and sold about 30 shops over the years, and copycats began copycatting. Teriyaki became ubiquitous, the Japanese name concealing its hometown heritage. Some locals don’t even realize teriyaki joints are a Seattle thing—that is, until they move elsewhere and try to find one.

Kitchens with Vietnamese roots began dishing up teriyaki alongside steaming bowlfuls of pho. Many spots still specialize in a classic interpretation, typically served with scoops of rice, some fried gyoza, and iceberg lettuce bathed in a thin mayo dressing. Enterprising Korean immigrants embraced teriyaki and opened their own outfits, adding bulgogi to the menu and gochujang to the chicken’s marinade.

The forward march of time, trends, and real estate prices means there’s sadly no longer a teriyaki business every few blocks. Those that remain include a few clunkers: Many have succumbed to shortcuts, serving sad chicken in gloopy, way-too-sweet gravy, which obscure the dish’s appeal to outsiders. But find a place still making its own sauce and blasting thighs on high heat, delivering bits of caramelized char that balance its teriyaki sweetness. Then you’ll understand.

Local wisdom dictates the best shop is the one closest to you, but here are eight greats, new and old.

Toshi Kasahara’s original restaurant, now long shuttered, was the archetype of a Seattle-style teriyaki spot—a spare cafeteria-like space with a streamlined menu built around Kasahara’s iconic chicken. Just a sprinkling of these shops still exist, but today only one is the real deal: a take-out operation deep in a Mill Creek strip mall. It’s open just a few hours in the evenings, with the 77-year-old Kasahara at the grill. He’s tweaked his methods slightly over the years, but his chicken is just as juicy and smoky as ever. No one in Seattle does it exactly like Toshi, but his sons do farther afield. One runs a Toshi’s food truck in San Francisco; the other is opening a Toshi’s outpost this winter in his father’s hometown of Ashikaga, Japan.

Hawaii has its own relationship to teriyaki. When restaurateur Matthew Parker opened his ode to the teriyaki counters that fueled his first 20 years in Seattle, he looked to his family’s roots in Oahu—specifically to huli huli chicken. That dish inspires Grillbird’s glossy house sauce, sweetened just enough with pineapple juice and ketchup. There’s no iceberg salad here; sides include mac salad and marinated cucumbers, dishes standard to plate lunch, Hawaii’s answer to the meat-and-three. Purists can grouse about how teriyaki shops should be old-school in every sense, but I welcome Grillbird’s modern touches, like online ordering and a mostly gluten-free menu. Grillbird’s original West Seattle outfit occupies a former Pizza Hut, which feels just right for this utilitarian dish. A second location in Phinney Ridge operates alongside sister concept Salad Party, for those looking to get their greens in.

When the Lee family lost the lease on their longtime teriyaki restaurant, the new location they’d scouted came with a catch: The strip mall that housed it already had a teriyaki shop. So matriarch Yoo-Mi Lee camouflaged her teriyaki menu with dishes from her Korean heritage and influences from the years the family lived in Brazil. Be thankful for that other teriyaki business, because Tá Jóia’s highly specific Brazilian-Korean-teriyaki remix is so vibrant and delicious, it could (should!) be a national fast-casual restaurant chain. Feijoada, a hearty slow-cooked black bean stew made with pork, bacon, and sausage, fits right in next to bulgogi, while the kitchen’s spectacular teriyaki hides in plain sight under the moniker “spicy chicken bowl.” It’s the chicken teriyaki of your hottest, most chili-spiked dreams, brightened with a scoop of pico and a drizzle of creamy house cilantro sauce.

No matter which member of the Kim family is behind the counter here, chances are they will offer you tea while you wait for your order. If the hospitality is great, the food is even better. Chicken teriyaki looks like it came off a photo shoot, deeply juicy with properly charred edges. It’s chicken that needs no supporting cast, but with so many combos on the menu, it’s fun to compare how the gingery sauce hits different proteins including beef, pork, prawn, or tofu. (If you’re exceedingly hungry, go for the formidable triple combo, which delivers chicken and beef teriyaki, golden-fried gyoza with a flaky, blistered exterior, and fragrant mounds of fried rice.) Teriyaki lovers are especially protective of Rainier Teriyaki since its late owner, Hansoo Kim, was tragically killed during a 2023 attempted armed robbery; the family banded together and reopened the restaurant in his honor.

Most people show up at Fremont’s busy donburi shop craving its chirashi bowl, but the chicken teriyaki imagines what Seattle’s signature dish might have looked like if it actually hailed from Japan. Butterflied thighs with the lightest of marinades come straight off the grill to be dressed with a sauce that’s thin by Seattle standards, but nonetheless lands a careful balance of savory and sweet. I appreciate this subtler rendition of chicken teriyaki, which complements an otherwise traditionally Japanese menu of rice bowls. Granted, people don’t usually crave Seattle teriyaki for its subtlety; add a dose of the house chili oil for texture and kick. Fremont Bowl is a kiosk-driven take-out machine, but the dine-in vibes are friendly, provided you can find a free table.

Ask a local about their favorite teriyaki shop, and chances are high it’s this been-there-forever counter next to a laundromat not far from Lake Union’s north end—not to be confused with other very similarly named Seattle teriyaki practitioners, including one on this list. A high ratio of dark soy makes for a standout sauce, while the thin mayo-based salad dressing plays well against the crispness of the fresh iceberg lettuce. The kitchen even uses an old-school mold to press rice into a pleasing half-football shape. Many teriyaki shops also have chicken katsu and egg rolls on the menu, but the versions here are standouts for their nongreasy crispy exteriors. The tables are mostly waiting zones for people ordering takeout, destined for a lunch in Gas Works Park, the nearby brewery taprooms, or just back to the surrounding tech offices. Come hungry: Portions are huge, even by generous teriyaki shop standards.

Nikko is busy most of the day, feeding a bustling lunch rush, teenagers after school, and evening take-out crowds. That turnover means teriyaki that’s always fresh, swiped with sauce that’s more soy than sugar and thick without verging on gummy. Jong Kwon and his family have run this West Seattle staple with warmth for more than two decades. Step inside the narrow shop and you’re transported back to Seattle’s era of peak teriyaki, a simpler time when one ordered off pictures on the wall rather than QR codes and the cashier remembered your name.

Clamshell take-out containers are so inherent to the teriyaki experience that nobody asks if you want your food to go, they generally just assume you do. But visit this Georgetown favorite (no relation to I Love Teriyaki) and you’ll witness a rare sight: Diners eating off actual plates. After a three-year closure following a fire, owners Don and Eva Lo rebuilt the original building (once a KFC) into a shiny new space. Aromas of grilled meat hit you from the parking lot, and the cheerful dining room is usually full. Skip the newish teriyaki burritos, and run, don’t walk, to the short ribs teriyaki, so smoky and tender that you might almost be tempted to bypass the chicken altogether. Almost.

#6638. Spiced Beef Baked Potatoes

Baked potatoes may not seem like a dish that requires much technique, but there’s a difference between a good baked potato and a great one. Wrapping them in foil can lead to a tender interior but render the skin too soft. For the most crisp skin, bake them right on the oven grate at quite a high temperature. (To make it taste almost like a potato chip, rub those scrubbed russets with vegetable oil and season with plenty of salt.) Shockingly, this doesn’t prevent a fluffy interior—that comes down to the internal temperature reaching at least 212°. Sure, it may seem strange to take your potato’s temperature, but it’s a fail-safe route to the most enjoyable potato.

Some, including the Idaho Potato Commission, swear that the way a baked potato is opened affects the texture, eschewing a knife for a fork to gently poke a plus sign into the surface. Others, like beloved food writer Nigel Slater, prefer to strike the potato as though it were part of a martial arts competition. “Bring your hand down fast and sharp as if you were doing a karate chop but only hard enough to crack open the potato skin,” he writes in a piece for The Guardian. (Whether or not to attempt this feat is literally in the hands of the potato-baker.) We found a single fork-pricked line down the length of the spud is the most effective.

Once opened, a baked potato can be filled with anything from tuna salad to cheesy baked beans. Here, it’s a picadillo-inspired mixture with ground beef (packed with protein, iron, and creatine—though ground turkey or chicken work nicely too) adorned with golden raisins and stuffed olives. A spicy tomato sauce will slowly soak into the potato, further seasoning it with every passing minute. Make sure to use a chili powder that’s a mix of spices like chiles, cumin, oregano, garlic (not just dried ground chiles).

Healthy cooking doesn’t have to be complicated. In fact, often the simpler it is, the better it tastes. In Good for You, Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firkser shares feel-good recipes for any day of the week. Read more: White Potatoes Are Not Empty Calories. They’re Actually Great for You.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 425°. Prick 4 large russet potatoes (about 10 oz. each), scrubbed, patted dry, all over with a fork, then rub all over with 1 Tbsp. vegetable oil and sprinkle with 1¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Bake directly on oven rack until skins are crisp and flesh is very soft (an instant-read thermometer inserted into the center should register 212°–220°), 55–75 minutes. (If thermometer registers 210° before beef mixture is finished, turn off oven and leave potatoes inside until ready to use.)

Meanwhile, pick enough leaves from ½ bunch cilantro (about 2 oz.) to measure ½ cup; set aside for serving. Finely chop remaining leaves and all of stems (you should have about ¾ cup); set aside separately.

Heat remaining 2 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large skillet over medium. Add 1 medium red or yellow onion, finely chopped, 5 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion is softened, 8–10 minutes. Add ¼ cup double-concentrated tomato paste and cook, stirring constantly, until deepened in color and slightly tacky, about 2 minutes.

Increase heat to medium-high. Add 1 lb. ground beef, 2 Tbsp. chili powder, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Cook, stirring and smashing often with a heatproof rubber spatula to break up meat, until cooked through, about 4 minutes.

Reduce heat to low. Add ½ cup golden raisins, ¼ cup sliced pimiento-stuffed green olives, reserved chopped cilantro, and 1 cup water. Cook, stirring occasionally, until sauce thickens slightly and flavors come together, 8–12 minutes. Taste beef mixture and season with more salt if needed. Remove from heat and cover. Let sit until ready to use.

Transfer potatoes to a platter or plates and let cool 5 minutes. Using a fork, prick a 3"–4"-long line in the center down length of each potato, leaving 1" unpricked on each end. Using your hands, firmly press ends down toward platter to split potatoes open. Smash flesh as desired, then season inside of potatoes with salt. Divide beef mixture among potatoes and top with reserved cilantro leaves.

#6637. The Beast in Me Season 2: Everything We Know So Far

Netflix’s The Beast in Me brought Claire Danes back to TV and reunited her with creator Howard Gordon, with whom she spent eight seasons working on Homeland. That combination was already exciting enough, but the cast also included Matthew Rhys and Brittany Snow, and Conan O’Brien and Jodie Foster were among the producers.

Danes stars as Aggie, a successful author grappling with the grief of losing her son. Her fragile sense of stability is shaken when Nile (Rhys), a wealthy real estate figure once accused of murdering his wife, moves in next door. With just eight episodes, the series left viewers wondering whether Aggie’s story could continue beyond its initial run. Here’s what we know so far.

Yes. In September 2026, Variety confirmed that The Beast in Me would return for a second season on Netflix.

“We always told ourselves we’d only do a second season of The Beast in Me if we found a story that was worthy of the first—and I’m thrilled to say we found it,” Gordon said in a statement. “We loved making this show and our audience seemed to love watching it, so we’re enormously grateful to Jinny Howe and Netflix, and to Karey Burke and 20th Television for giving us the chance to get the band back together and do it again.”

Variety’s report confirmed that Danes would return to her role for The Beast in Me season 2. In October 2026, Deadline reported that John Goodman (Righteous Gemstones, Digger) would star as “Aggie’s dad, believed to be a long-time con artist.”

In November 2026, Deadline revealed that Lili Taylor (Outer Range, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping) joined the cast in a series regular role as Fiona, Aggie’s stepmother.

Gordon discussed the ending of season 1 with The Wrap and what it made him consider for season 2.

“I think that to the extent that Aggie is a writer who has been delivered to this next stage of her life, whatever that stage is,” he shared at the time. “If there is a story, there might be more. I am tempted by the character of her grifter father in some way. We’ll see how the show does and if an idea comes. But I think they’d be open to more.”

#6636. A Night of Firsts: The History-Making Victories Across the 2026 Midterm Elections

It took 94 years for Kansas to elect another Democratic U.S. senator. It took the entire history of the United States for a Black woman to be elected governor. Both happened on Tuesday night—two significant milestones amid a night of major triumphs, firsts, and history-making moments.

The 2026 midterm elections delivered a political earthquake, with a series of candidates and statewide contests drawing national attention. Democrats reclaimed control of both chambers of Congress, flipping seven Senate seats—including in Republican strongholds where the party had not won in decades. In Georgia, Keisha Lance Bottoms became the first Black woman elected governor in American history. In New Mexico, Deb Haaland became the first Native American woman elected to lead a state, while Minnesota’s Peggy Flanagan became the first Native American woman elected to the U.S. Senate. Michigan elected the country’s first Muslim senator, Abdul El-Sayed, and New Hampshire its first openly gay male senator, Chris Pappas. And longstanding political barriers fell elsewhere—from Texas electing its first Latina governor to Florida electing its first Black governor, Republican Byron Donalds.

And it was true that the gubernatorial races sent shockwaves from state to state. In California, Xavier Becerra, the former U.S. secretary of health and human services, became the first Latino ever elected governor of the state. And both Nevada and Wisconsin elected their first Black governors: Attorney General Aaron Ford and Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, respectively. Minnesota elected its first woman governor in Amy Klobuchar, who will leave behind her seat in the U.S. Senate after two decades. And in Ohio, former state health director Amy Acton defeated Republican Vivek Ramaswamy to become the first woman elected governor in the state’s history.

The Democratic gains were impressive across states where Republicans have dominated for years. In Iowa, state auditor Rob Sand became the first Democrat elected governor since 2006. In Kansas, Adam Hamilton defeated incumbent Roger Marshall to become the first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from the state since 1932. South Carolina delivered another seismic upset as pediatrician Annie Andrews became the first Democrat to win a Senate election there since 1998—and the first woman ever elected to represent the state in the upper chamber. Former North Carolina governor Roy Cooper ended an 18-year Democratic Senate drought, and in Texas, state representative James Talarico became the first Democrat elected to the Senate since 1988, defeating Republican Ken Paxton.

There were significant victories further down the ballot, too. In Alabama, Democrat Allison Montgomery defeated Republican incumbent Phillip Rigsby to become the state’s first openly transgender lawmaker. The software engineer and LGBTQ+ rights advocate campaigned on issues including public education, healthcare, and affordability, despite facing dogged attacks on her gender identity from her opponent. In Indiana, 30-year-old Beau Bayh, the son of former governor and senator Evan Bayh and grandson of former senator Birch Bayh, became the first Democrat to win statewide office since 2012, defeating Republican Max Engling in the race for secretary of state.

Across the country, people voted in the midterm elections to significantly expand who holds power in America, all over a single night in which decades of political precedent were overturned.

#6635. What You Need to Know About Volufiline, Everyone’s Latest Skin Care Obsession

Social media is full of products that promise to transform your face. The latest one making the rounds? Volufiline, an ingredient being likened to natural filler. Guys are swiping and dabbing it onto their undereyes, smile lines, and lips in the hopes of restoring volume and looking younger with no needles, lasers, or scalpels in sight. Fans credit the topical for improvements in undereye hollows and skin quality and making them get carded again. One X user even claims that it looks like “you’ve genuinely gotten a facelift” after two weeks of use.

The pitch is that Volufiline is basically filler in a bottle. But does it actually check out?

Volufiline is a trademarked cosmetic ingredient made with Anemarrhena asphodeloides root extract (a source of the compound sarsasapogenin) and hydrogenated polyisobutene (an emollient that softens and smooths skin). “The theory is that sarsasapogenin encourages fat cells to develop and store more lipids, making them fuller,” says Kseniya Kobets, MD, director of cosmetic dermatology at Montefiore Einstein Advanced Care. Essentially, the hope is to counteract volume loss that naturally occurs as we grow older.

We’ve spent the last year sampling the latest releases in men’s skin care, hair care, and more. Our favorites will help you level up.

In a small study by Sederma, the French company that manufactures Volufiline, 28 women applied a cream containing Volufiline to one breast for 56 days. While the treated breast’s average volume increased by 2.2%, the result wasn’t statistically significant. Kobets also points out that the comparison was with an untreated breast—rather than the same cream without Volufiline—so it’s unclear if Volufiline or other ingredients in the cream drove the increase in volume. Plus, we can’t exactly extrapolate the results seen in a female breast to a man’s face.

Despite the lack of robust clinical evidence supporting its anti-aging claims, Volufiline is the latest topical du jour that people are crediting with their plumper, more supple skin—namely in areas prone to volume loss like the undereyes, smile lines, cheeks, and lips. Some before-and-afters on social media are visually compelling. But the bigger question is whether Volufiline meaningfully increases facial volume or if the improvements are simply due to a temporary plumping effect—or even the other ingredients paired alongside it.

“Some improvement likely comes from the moisturizing formula: hydration softens fine lines, emollients smooth the surface, and that finish changes how light reflects off skin,” Kobets says. (Changes in lighting and specific camera angles can also make the after photos look more striking.) While Volufiline might help your skin look better, the jury’s still out on whether it meaningfully restores lost volume. “Making skin look hydrated and plump isn’t the same as rebuilding the fat underneath it,” Kobets says.

As for those filler in a bottle claims? Alexandra Bowles, DO, a board-certified dermatologist at MONA Dermatology, sets the record straight. “Volufiline is designed to support volume in the skin, and some people may notice slightly plumper, fuller-looking skin over time,” she says. Meanwhile, injectable filler adds immediate volume and structure and can reshape areas like the tear trough, lips, and jawline. “A cream or serum works at the surface and builds gradually, so it can’t create that kind of change,” she says. Read: While it may complement your skin care routine, it won’t replace or replicate results from filler.

Both derms are open to patients experimenting with Volufiline, but with a few caveats. “I think Volufiline is worth trying if you have realistic expectations, but it’s definitely overhyped as an alternative to filler,” Bowles says. If you really want to (pardon the pun) move the needle on undereye hollows, loss of lip volume, or a less-defined jawline, she says carefully placed filler or other in-office treatments may be more effective.

Kobets doesn’t rule out trying Volufiline, either, so long as you’re not expecting to restore facial fat. That said, she advises being cautious if you have a chronic skin condition like eczema or rosacea, or if you’re acne-prone. Try a patch test first and stop if your skin stings or burns.

Bowles suggests prioritizing reputable brands with clear ingredient lists and modest claims around a gradual improvement in the look and feel of skin. Be wary of products that promise instant results, have vague ingredient lists, or come from unverified sellers. “Don’t experiment with raw ingredients or assume a higher percentage works better,” Kobets adds.

The TL;DR: Volufiline is intriguing, but the hype is outpacing the evidence. More rigorous research is needed to address its volume-enhancing claims for facial skin, so take them with a grain of salt. Consistently using a well-formulated product might help your skin look more supple and hydrated; just don’t expect any miracles or a true dupe for injectables. “Good skin care improves skin quality, but it can’t do every job we’re asking of it,” Kobets says.

#6634. Colin Jost Takes Gift-Giving Seriously

The Weekend Update co-host and Kay campaign star shares his approach to holiday shopping.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Finding the perfect holiday gift isn’t easy. Between the pressure to get it right, the endless wish lists, and the people who insist they don’t want anything, shopping for loved ones can feel like an impossible mission. Even Colin Jost, who has spent years navigating the pressures of live television, admits that the process is incredibly stressful.

This festive season, the Weekend Update co-host is putting his comedic talents to work with Kay by starring in the jeweler’s latest holiday campaign, “Love All In.” The cheeky ad follows Jost on an increasingly ridiculous quest to find the perfect present, poking fun at the lengths we’ll go to for the people closest to us. It’s a fitting partnership for someone who knows a thing or two about making people laugh but also takes gifting pretty seriously.

“I think I’m a good gift giver,” Jost tells ELLE. “Giving gifts is stressful because I do want it to be a meaningful gift. I hate the idea of just buying something because you have to give someone something.”

For Jost, the secret to getting it right has less to do with how much you spend and more to do with how much thought goes into it. “At every kind of price point for any gift, there [are] thoughtful and unthoughtful versions,” he says. “Something can be really expensive but not thoughtful.”

It’s a sentiment that aligns with Kay’s latest campaign, which encourages shoppers to go “all in” when expressing their love. And while Jost might not be the first person you’d think to turn to for jewelry advice, he’s developed an appreciation for it over the years, thanks to his very chic wife, Scarlett Johansson.

“Until five years ago, I didn’t own a watch,” he admits. That changed when the actress gifted him his first one, introducing him to an entirely new world of accessories. As for whether she’s influenced his personal style? “In that it’s exclusively managed by her, yes, I would say she’s influenced it.”

Despite his Staten Island roots, Jost’s jewelry preferences are surprisingly understated. “I don’t really wear a ton of jewelry, but I also am from Staten Island, so I do have to have certain pieces, or else they won’t let me back over the Verrazano Bridge,” he jokes.

While browsing Kay’s assortment, he found himself drawn to simple gold pieces, including a ring, bracelet, and necklace. “They were really nice, but also they weren’t gaudy or anything,” he says. His preference for gold also comes with some rather unconventional reasoning: “If we get into a post-apocalyptic situation, it feels like it’s better to melt down for trading.”

When it comes to shopping for the people closest to him, Jost admits that both Johansson and his Weekend Update collaborator Michael Che are difficult to buy things for, though he found a creative solution for the latter. “I got Che a really large and heavy, realistic statue of a velociraptor,” he recalls. “It was so heavy that he literally can’t get rid of it.” The real expense wasn’t the dinosaur itself. “The main cost was shipping,” he says. “It was a huge eyesore, and it’s prohibitively expensive for him to have removed from his property.”

The hardest person to gift on Jost’s list? His father, who insists he doesn’t need anything. “I think he actually means it, but it’s so unhelpful,” Jost says. After years of nostalgic gifts inspired by his dad’s past, he’s running out of ideas. “I’ve got to figure out something that breaks through his defenses.”

In terms of gifting etiquette, Jost has a few rules of his own. For starters, he’s big on surprises. While he understands the appeal of a wish list for children, he thinks adults should leave a little room for the unexpected. “For adults, it’s got to be ‘surprise me,’” he says. “The surprise is half the fun, three-quarters of the fun.” Regifting, on the other hand, comes with a few conditions. He’s open to the idea, but only if the gift is a perfect fit for someone and there’s full disclosure.

But perhaps the most surprising revelation comes when I ask what’s on his own holiday wish list. After spending much of our conversation discussing what to buy everyone else, Jost seems relieved to finally be on the receiving end. “Oh, thank you! Finally, someone asked me. What do I want?”

His answer? Nothing material. “At this point in life, I mostly want experiences,” he says. Whether it’s a trip or simply someone taking the initiative to organize an outing, he’s more interested in making memories than collecting more things. “Even if it’s just the plan of, ‘Let’s go do this at this time,’ I think that’s a great gift.” Or, when in doubt, a velociraptor.

#6632. Toasted Meringue Hazelnut Blondies

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Lightly coat a 9x9" pan with nonstick vegetable oil spray. Line pan with parchment paper, leaving overhang on two sides. Toast 2 cups blanched hazelnuts on a rimmed baking sheet, tossing halfway through, until golden brown and fragrant, 15–18 minutes. Let sit until cool enough to handle, then coarsely chop; set aside.

Cook 1 cup (2 sticks) unsalted butter in a small saucepan over medium heat, stirring often, until butter foams, then browns (do not burn), 7–9 minutes. Remove from heat.

Whisk 2 large eggs, room temperature, 1 large egg yolk, room temperature, 1¼ cups (250 g) granulated sugar, ¼ cup (packed; 50 g) light brown sugar, 2 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ¾ tsp. instant espresso powder (if using) in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment on medium-high speed until mixture is pale and doubled in volume, 6–9 minutes (mixture will form an unbroken ribbon when whisk is lifted from bowl).

Reduce speed to low and with motor running, gradually pour in brown butter in a thin, continuous stream; beat until incorporated, about 2 minutes. Remove bowl from mixer and gently fold in 1½ cups (187 g) all-purpose flour with a rubber spatula, scraping down sides and bottom of bowl, until no large, dry streaks of flour remain. Scrape batter into prepared pan; smooth surface. Top with reserved hazelnuts and press in gently to adhere (surface will be smothered with nuts).

Bake blondie until edges are golden brown and center is just set, 35–45 minutes. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let blondie cool in pan. Using parchment paper to help, lift blondie out of pan and transfer to rack.

Meanwhile, combine 3 large egg whites and 1 cup (200 g) granulated sugar in the clean bowl of stand mixer and set over a saucepan of just simmering water (make sure bottom of bowl does not touch water). Heat, whisking constantly, until sugar is dissolved and an instant-read thermometer registers 170°.

Fit bowl onto mixer fitted with clean whisk attachment. Beat egg white mixture until thick and glossy and mixture is barely lukewarm, 8–10 minutes. Add 1 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt; fold in with a rubber spatula just to combine. Taste meringue and season with more kosher salt if needed

Peel away parchment paper from blondie and transfer to a heatproof platter. Using an offset spatula, spread meringue evenly over blondie, covering from edge to edge. Using a kitchen torch, toast meringue until deep golden brown. Sprinkle with flaky sea salt. Using a long knife and wiping off with a damp kitchen towel between cuts, slice blondie into 9 squares.

Do Ahead: Blondie can be baked 24 hours ahead. Store, loosely covered, at room temperature.

#6631. 8 Delicious Host Gifts That Aren’t Wine

“What should I bring?” When a guest asks this well-intentioned question, the knee-jerk answer is “Wine!” But it’s just as simple to source thoughtful bits and bobs to create a memorable start to the meal. This way the host can forget about hors d’oeuvres altogether. Pick up a bark-wrapped cheese, artfully marbled charcuterie, or some I-can’t-believe-it’s-store-bought spritzes—or better yet, all of the above—and your fellow diners will be asking where they can buy a box on the way home.

If you are looking to contribute an NA option to the bar, you can’t do better than Ghia’s most recent release, Le Spritz Blood Orange. It’s a bubbly mix of bitter and sweet that more than fills in for an Aperol spritz or predinner glass of prosecco.

The problem with baked Brie is you have to bake it. Instead, bring a soft-rind cheese that can hold its own weight. Set it out on a plate or board for up to an hour before serving; this variety is best eaten at room temp when it’s soft and spreadable and the flavors have bloomed. St. Stephen from Four Fat Fowl in upstate New York is a triple-cream so buttery that even kids will go for seconds. Rush Creek Reserve is a dippable fondue-like wheel wrapped in spruce bark from Uplands in Dodgeville, WI.

The phrase “melts in your mouth” may be oft used and infrequently true, yet the ultramarbled Paleta from Campo Grande actually does. The thinly sliced Ibérico pork shoulder, aged for three years, is Hall of Fame charcuterie board fare. After you set it on the coffee table, don’t walk away, because it’ll be gone by the time you get back.

It’s never been easier to bring quality, ethically sourced caviar to the party. There are lots of sites that will send fish eggs to your door starting around $100. One of our favorites comes from the folks at Island Creek Oysters in Duxbury, MA. They hand-pack their Italian White Sturgeon Caviar and offer next-day shipping. Set out your tin with a thick potato chip (we like Graza or North Fork) and something dairy-rich and creamy (might we recommend labneh?) to balance the brine.

A toasted baguette on bottom, Fishwife’s Cantabrian Anchovies on top, two ways to complete the tartine: Spread a fun cultured butter (we like Frentel, often available at Whole Foods) and you have a classic pintxo. Or, double up on tinned ingredients by adding a layer of Row 7 Sweet Prince Tomatoes and you get a gussied-up pan con tomate.

#6629. Kate Moss Proves the Leather Midi Skirt Is Eternally Appealing

Moss has always got a new way to make a classic item feel fresh.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Kate Moss is era-defining—as synonymous with the look of Cool Britannia in the ’90s as she is with Indie Sleaze. And yet, when you take apart Moss’s wardrobe, it’s clear to see that the supermodel has always stuck to the classics. Case in point: her look to attend Tom Ford’s SS27 show during Paris Fashion Week on September 30.

The 52-year-old arrived in support of her friend and the brand’s creative director, Haider Ackermann, wearing a tried-and-tested formula of a button-down Oxford shirt and sleek and shiny leather pencil skirt. Her take was loaded with sex appeal and timeless allure in equal measure.

The brilliance of Moss’s look came in its application. She’s always been great at styling familiar pieces in inventive ways to bring them back into rotation. Here, she left her shirt open entirely and rolled up the sleeves, with the high waist of the skirt stepping in at just the right point. Her choice of a string bra kept things feeling more contemporary than the more obvious choice of something lacy, perhaps. Sunglasses for the nighttime added A-list appeal, while her green stone ring reminded us of her often bohemian style sensibility. The final touch of strappy sandals finished Moss’s look with the sky-high heels she often turns to.

The cut of the skirt was key, too. Its pencil shape added to that classic ideal of sex-appeal dressing, feeling typically true of Tom Ford’s design signature that Ackermann now does his own way. It’s a shape that never goes out of style, whether it’s worn like Moss or in contrast with a roomy wool jumper or a lacy camisole.

It’s the skirt of the season. How will you wear yours?

#6628. Frico'ed Brussels Sprouts

A slick of oil and a sprinkling of salt are the only adornments brussels sprouts need to shine. But put a crispy Parmesan skirt on them and suddenly the humble veggie becomes the belle of the ball. This recipe does just that. By roasting the brussels sprouts snuggled into a blanket of grated Parmesan cheese, the cheese melts into a crispy, frico-like sheet that clings onto the sprouts, surrounding them in a lace-like halo. It’s a dramatic side dish, but one that makes a serious statement. If roasted correctly, and the stars align in your favor, you can peel off the entire sheet in one swift swoop, presenting it as the culinary masterpiece it is. Fans of fun, this is for you.

It’s That Simple is our series about recipes so easy, you can make them with your eyes closed. Think tiny ingredient lists, laid-back techniques, and results so delicious you’ll text home about them. Read more: Your Brussels Sprouts Need a Crispy, Cheesy Skirt.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 400°. Line a baking sheet with a nonstick baking mat or a sheet of parchment paper generously coated with nonstick vegetable oil spray. Toss 1½ lb. brussels sprouts, trimmed, halved, 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper in a medium bowl to combine. Scatter 4 oz. store-bought grated Parmesan (pre-grated works better here than grating from a block) in an even layer over baking sheet, leaving a ½" border around edges. Arrange brussels sprouts, cut side down, in a single layer on top, spacing evenly to fill baking sheet. Bake until brussels sprouts are tender and browned and cheese is deep golden, 20–28 minutes. (If the cheese in the very center is browned, it’s done.) Let cool at least 5 minutes, then break into pieces to serve. (Or place another parchment-lined baking sheet upside down on top; holding together, swiftly turn over, peel away mat, and present cheese side up.)

#6625. Book Breakfasts, Babysitters, and the Russian Tea Room: A Day With Author Tarajia Morrell

Forget 9-to-5. Mothering knows no schedule—often it feels more like 5-to-9 and everything in between. In this series, we look at the hectic, messy, sometimes beautiful, often frustrating enterprise of being a mother—and maintaining a life of your own. Consider it a “day in the life” for the forgotten hours.

Today, we’re following Tarajia Morrell, the James Beard Award–winning food writer, author, and communications consultant. Her new memoir, Desire Feeds the Feast, is out now. The book is a rich and lyrical telling of her childhood as the daughter of a dynasty of Manhattan wine sellers; her days on the New York City club scene of the late ’90s; her culinary studies, acting auditions, and restaurant jobs; and more.

A single mother, Morrell lives in her childhood home—a rent-stabilized Manhattan apartment that she fought for and won—with her five-year-old daughter, Viva. On a recent Thursday, she brought Vogue along for a busy day, which included everything from the school bus stop and a book breakfast to a podcast taping, a party, and the realities of mealtime. (“Indeed, I am a food writer whose child is a picky eater,” she writes.)

My alarm goes off. Immediately, I recall that today is not a normal day at my desk at home, writing copy for the hotels for which I’m the communications director. Today is a day in which I must also focus on my book, and it’s going to be a doozy.

I go make myself some jet fuel. While the coffee pot is on the stove, I turn on my morning music: Alice Coltrane Radio on Spotify, which both soothes and invigorates me at once with its harp and organ. It’s still almost completely dark out, but, from the living room, I can see the first blush of light above a little slice of the 59th Street Bridge. This sight (and the coffee) has its usual effect: I have a jolt of how lucky I am to be exactly where I am—in this home with this child.

It’s been a challenge to pry Viva from sleep for her new kindergarten wake-up time, so I am delightfully surprised when I open the door to her tiny bedroom (the tiny bedroom of my childhood!) and she’s sitting in front of her dollhouse at play. Blaring Alice Coltrane and Éthiopiques is clearly an excellent, calming way to start her day too.

Viva colors while she eats her breakfast of a cinnamon-raisin English muffin with Nutella (I know, I know), berries, and juice. Indeed, I am a food writer whose child is a picky eater. A predawn morning is not the hour to prove points.

I help Viva dress for school even though I am supposed to let her do it entirely independently. My excuse is that time is of the essence, but that’s true in more ways than one. I stare at her long, lithe limbs and wonder where my chubby baby has gone. Since having her, time has changed. It used to be something that haunted me with its slow creep; now I am always chasing more of it.

Our school bus is meant to arrive at 7:22 but is always outrageously early or late. I receive a text from the dad of an older girl who also gets picked up at our stop, saying “The bus is running early,” so I grab a coat and Viva’s things and we dash. As we make our way, I feel enormously grateful for this relative stranger whose tiny updates help my life be less stressful. As a parent in general, but particularly as a solo parent, supportive gestures that help the wheels stay on (and help me avoid a school run) are more appreciated that I can express.

We do a weird little dance while we wait, with Viva basically inside my coat for warmth and cuddles. The song I hum is vaguely reminiscent of the Beverly Hills Cop theme song. I don’t care what I look like in these stolen silly moments of just being her mother.

Back home and I hop in the shower. My literary agent, Andy McNicol, is picking me up to go to a breakfast hosted at Claudette by owner Carlos Suarez on lower Fifth to celebrate my memoir, Desire Feeds the Feast.

Andy is right on time and we head downtown. Twenty minutes into the ride, I ask the driver why we skipped our exit off the FDR, and it turns out that it’s because he has the wrong address. I tease Andy about typing without wearing her glasses. One of the many indignities of aging is that none of us seem to be able to see without our glasses.

We arrive at Claudette and I instantly feel more calm. Writing the book has been a very solitary experience—done after Viva falls asleep—and finally getting to squeeze my pals and feel less alone in it is a balm to my nerves.

So many people I love are here from many chapters of my life, and an adorable number of them are wearing red and black—a clear nod to my book cover—as am I. My friend Batsheva Hay clocks my dress and asks if it’s vintage Geoffrey Beene. We both laugh: She’d had her eye on the same one on The RealReal. I am the geek who enjoys matching my book cover. Plus there’s a great vintage Geoffrey Beene scene in the book (i.e., in my life), so it feels pleasantly full circle.

The breakfast ends and I prepare to depart for the rest of my day. I tucked jeans into my bag, but, unfortunately, I forgot to put in a shirt. Classic me to find myself in this predicament on a day that I am reporting to, ahem, Vogue. I put on my leather jacket without a shirt underneath and go hunting for a T-shirt before my next rendezvous. Save Khaki United on Greenwich Avenue seems like the best and closest option, and sure enough, I find a perfect simple long-sleeve T-shirt there.

I meet creative director Anna Polonsky at the new Santo Taco on Carmine, where she’s overseeing a photo shoot with Gentl and Hyers of the food and space. Anna and I have done branding projects together for both Troutbeck and Belden House & Mews, the sister hotels with which I work. We catch up over agua frescas and divine tacos and discuss branding for Firehouse—the soon-to-open membership and events space for Belden. We soon discover we will also both be at the same event later that night; love it when that happens.

I fly by The Strand, the legendary bookstore where I am launching my book on November 4 (!), and its events director greets me for a quick tour of the room I’ll be in. I am completely verklempt to see my book on little posters, including on the elevator. I’m pinching myself…even more so when I am taken to the greenroom and see the walls covered in photos of my literary idols who have read there.

I walk up Broadway to the Malin to meet Angela Ledgerwood of the podcast Lit Up to record an episode on my book. We also did one for Savor: A Chef’s Hunger for More, which I coauthored with Fatima Ali, and since our last recording session, Angela married a friend of mine from high school. They’ve become winemakers, launching Old Sound Vineyard on the North Fork. If insomnia and needing glasses are drawbacks of getting older, one of the enormous pleasures is this sort of happenstance: people you love finding love with people you love.

I take the R train downtown to meet Charlie Champalimaud, an owner of Troutbeck and Belden, at Thompson Street Studio, where artist Kiva Motnyk has her more commercial practice. Charlie has commissioned a work by Kiva for Belden, so we go to see sketches for it and discuss timing for delivery. I learn that Kiva grew up in the building we are in, which feels like another good omen, since my book is about unexpectedly finding myself in the New York City apartment in which I began.

I am properly zonked. I consider a taxi but despise being stuck in traffic and the absurd prices, so I get on the R at Prince Street and start to tackle my neglected emails. I am so distracted and fried that I forget to switch to the Q and accidentally go to Queens instead of 86th Street. Amateur hour. I take the train back to Manhattan and hail a cab to make up for lost time.

I pick Viva up and we head home. I ask her what she had for lunch at school, and she tells me “applesauce, french fries, and broccoli.” Super.

Home. Quick dinner of “crispy chicken,” which is hammered panko and egg-battered chicken breasts that I made the night before and is no longer crispy, blanched broccoli (Viva’s requested veg for the night, despite its presence at lunch), and avocado with sea salt.

The lovely sitter arrives and immediately engages Viva in an art project. Nothing is normal this month of book launch and tour, and it would be impossible without my mother and support system of other mom friends helping enormously. I am so tired that when I sit down for a moment of sunshine on the terrace, I consider bailing on my plans for the evening, but the sitter is already here.

I arrive at Le Monde Beryl’s new shop on 67th Street for a cocktail party cohosted by The Perfect. One of my oldest friends, Lily Hanbury, started LMB 10 years ago with Katya Shifrin, and they’ve just opened this stunning store designed by Silka Rittson-Thomas. I live in Le Monde Beryl shoes because I can walk everywhere fast in them (Viva calls fast walking “city walking,” which I love). I am wearing a long silk dress by DeMeric, really chosen for my next and final stop, so am a bit dressed up for the cocktail at LMB, but old buddies and immediate laughter (with me? at me?) make it irrelevant.

I arrive on that strange crest of 57th Street to the Russian Tea Room, which is celebrating 100 years. I’m in a room with my food world family…as well as the trademark bawdy ice sculptures, gilt details, and red patina. I try to recall the last time I was here. I think it was 1999, at a dinner with Paris Hilton before a wild evening at a nightclub.

My exhaustion hits me hard. We restaurant folk commence our usual conversation of where we can go to get food immediately, and I suggest Dim Sum Palace, around the corner on 56th. It is not a palace, but it is a great place to go when you’re starving with six friends and no reservation at 8:30 on a gorgeous autumnal Thursday.

Home. When you parent alone, a babysitter who puts things in the dishwasher is like winning the lottery. I climb into the loft bed that was once mine and kiss my child, pulling the covers she’s kicked off back over her. As I fall asleep in my own bed, I am thinking of how well our home fits us—a mother and child, just us. It’s still pretty unfathomable that I lived in this fabulous but not so large apartment with two parents until I was 15. My last thought is to marvel at the strangeness of it all, the gift of it, being here with her. All this searching, hunger, and marveling is what drove me to write the book. Good night.
