#6598. 32 Makeup Gift Sets Every Beauty Lover Will Obsess Over

Somewhere between the first holiday party invite and the moment you realize November is already a quarter of the way gone, your gift list starts growing on its own. The good news? Presents from the beauty category make it a lot more manageable. They’re easy to shop, they’re hard to get wrong, and everyone in your life could use a few more of them, whether they like to admit it or not.

It can be as simple as a lipstick in a case they’ll want to show off, or as big as the LED mask they’ve had in their shopping cart for months now. And there’s plenty to love in between, from skin care they’d never splurge on for themselves and makeup gift sets to a beauty tool or two that turn the bathroom into something close to a visit to the facialist.

Every year, the same people are the hardest to shop for: the mom who insists she doesn’t need anything, the sister with impossibly specific taste, the friend who has genuinely tried it all. This list has them covered, along with a few names you’ll probably add later. Keep scrolling to shop the best beauty gifts and thank yourself in mid-December when you’re crowned best gift giver ever.

The best makeup gifts are the ones most people wouldn’t buy for themselves, like a designer lipstick in a case nice enough to leave out on the vanity, or a set of minis that finally gets someone to try a brand they’ve been curious about. This year’s holiday sets lean right into that, with limited-edition shades and packaging that looks just as good on a dresser as it does wrapped under the tree. Whether the person on your list does a full face every morning or rarely gets past mascara, there’s something here for them.

It’s hard to go wrong with Chanel, and this set is all about the small details that make someone feel put=together. Tucked inside a limited-edition white pouch with a soft, knitlike texture, it includes the Rouge Coco Baume Satin tinted lip balm, which goes on sheer and builds to lipstick-like color with a few more swipes, plus one of the brand’s hand creams and a bottle of the Le Vernis nail polish in the classic shade Ballerina.

For the person who treats their makeup bag like an accessory, this one comes in a sleek metallic clutch that’s chic enough to carry on its own. Inside, there’s Prada’s Pradascope mascara for lifted, clump-free lashes; the refillable Monochrome lipstick in Tiepolo, a soft, diffused matte finish; plus two lip balm refills in Universal and Astral Pink that keep lips comfortable for up to 24 hours.

For the friend who always has their trusty lip liner handy, you can’t go wrong with this set. Makeup artist (and Vogue Beauty Board member) Fara Homidi’s Smudge & Contour pencils are a cult favorite, designed with a creamy, almost balmy feel, so they glide on without dragging, and can be smudged out with a fingertip or sculpted into perfection with a makeup brush. The brand’s holiday trio comes in three neutrals, a cool beige, a taupe, and a deep brown, covering everything from a barely-there line to a deeper, more defined lip.

If someone on your list always runs late to holiday parties, they’re in luck, because we’ve uncovered the perfect gift for them. Gucci Westman picked the four products she’d reach for with only a few minutes to get ready, and all four come in mini sizes that slip easily into an evening bag. A cherry red blush stick and a rosy-taupe highlighter take care of the cheeks, while a charcoal eye pencil and Westman’s buildable mascara handle the eyes, so the whole look comes together fast.

In our opinion, skin care is one of the easier things to gift, since almost everyone has a routine, and most people are quietly hoping someone will hand them the moisturizer or serum they’ve been too practical to buy for themselves. The best picks this season either upgrade a step someone already loves or introduce them to a brand they’ve been curious about, and a few come in packaging nice enough that the box doesn’t even need wrapping.

Sulwhasoo has built its name on ginseng, and this set is the easiest way to see why. It includes the brand’s full-size Concentrated Ginseng Rejuvenating Cream along with smaller sizes of the matching eye cream, serum, and cleansing foam, so the whole routine is covered from start to finish.

This is the moisturizer to give the person who has tried everything. Dr. Diamond’s HYDR/O is a sheer cream that sinks in quickly but delivers serious hydration, thanks to a long list of hyaluronic acids, ceramides, and squalane that help strengthen the skin barrier over time.

Dieux’s got loyal fans for a reason, and this kit pairs two of its most popular products in one, reusable and decorative tin. The full-size Deliverance Serum helps calm redness and soften the look of wrinkles and dark spots, while a mini Instant Angel Moisturizer locks in moisture and leaves skin dewy enough to wear under makeup. Both are fragrance-free and gentle enough for sensitive skin, so it’s an easy gift even if you’re not sure what someone’s routine looks like.

For the friend who loves a Sunday night face mask, this set is basically a week of spa nights in one box. It includes five of 111Skin’s sheet masks, each one targeting something different, from hydration and brightening to depuffing, plus a lifting mask for the neck. Each takes about 20 minutes, and at a $161 value, it’s a fun way to try the brand’s bestsellers and find out which one is best for you.

Beauty tools tend to be the gifts people secretly want most and are least likely to buy themselves, mostly because the price tags make it hard to justify. That’s exactly what makes them such a good present. This year’s picks bring the kind of treatments you’d normally book at a dermatologist’s office or a facialist into the bathroom at home, from LED masks and laser caps to a hydro-facial that takes about 10 minutes.

Currentbody’s LED masks already have a cult following, and the Series 3 is its most advanced yet. It packs 750 LED bulbs and six different wavelengths, including red and near-infrared light for firmness and fine lines, and blue light for breakouts. The brand’s MyDose technology works out the right treatment for your skin, and there are four preset modes if you’d rather not think about it. A touch-screen controller with a countdown timer makes it easy to stick with, which matters, since LED works best with consistent use.

For anyone dealing with thinning hair, this is one of the most serious tools you can give them. The Capillus Spectrum looks like a regular baseball cap, but inside, it uses red and infrared lasers to stimulate hair follicles, and it’s FDA-cleared to treat hereditary hair loss in both men and women. It only takes six minutes a day, and the cap shuts itself off when the session is done, so it’s easy to wear while you answer email or make coffee.

Think of this as a facialist that fits in your hand. HigherDose’s just-debuted wand pairs a cold laser with red, near-infrared, and blue LED light, so it can help firm and smooth fine lines on one setting and calm breakouts and redness on another. A cooling attachment swaps on to depuff under-eyes and sculpt along the jawline, and most sessions take 10 to 15 minutes. It even comes with a travel case, plus minis of the brand’s peptide serum and facial mist to prep skin first.

For the person on your list who splurges on a biweekly or monthly facial, the Shark Beauty FacialPro is most likely sitting high on their wish list. An easy way to unclog and clean pores plus infuse skin with powerful ingredients like hyaluronic acid, this gift takes its owner into the driver’s seat, giving them the power of visiting their favorite spa right at home.

Hair gifts are a safe bet for almost anyone, since even people who barely think about their routine still have a shampoo they’re loyal to or a styling tool they’ve been eyeing for months. From a splurge-worthy straightener that skips the hot plates entirely to travel-size sets that are perfect for stuffing into a carry-on, there’s something for the person who does their own personal blowout every morning and the one who simply wants their strands to feel soft.

Anyone who’s ever waited for their hair to dry before reaching for a flatiron will understand the appeal here. Dyson’s Airstrait dries and straightens at the same time, using airflow instead of hot plates, so you can go from towel-dried hair to a sleek, finished look with one tool. It has three heat settings and a separate mode for touching up dry hair, and the arms lock together so you can rough-dry your roots first. It’s a splurge, but it cuts out an entire step of the routine.

If holding a round brush and a dryer at the same time has never worked out for you, this is the fix. Wavytalk’s thermal brush works on dry hair, so you get the volume and bend of a blowout from a single tool, with five heat settings up to 420° F and a ceramic barrel that heats evenly. Negative ions help keep frizz down, and since it’s dual-voltage, it’s easy to pack for trips abroad.

As frustrating as it can be, you can’t reach your hair goals if you don’t repair damage first. If your giftee has been trying to assuage breakage, heat damage, or dry and brittle strands, Redken’s Acidic Bonding collection is like the golden ticket. Powered by Bonding Care Complex and citric acid, these products are formulated to reinforce weakened or broken bonds for smoother, stronger hair—and even protect hair color from fading.

For the person in your life who’s always on a plane, this set from RŌZ packs a full routine into carry-on-friendly sizes. The masterwork of celebrity hairstylist and Vogue Beauty Board member Mara Roszak, this set includes the Foundation Shampoo and Conditioner, the Santa Lucia Styling Oil for frizz and shine, and the Milk Hair Serum, a leave-in that works whether you air-dry or blow-dry. Plus, everything is sulfate-free and smells as good as it performs.

Yes, buying perfume for someone else can feel like a gamble, since what smells amazing on you might not work on them at all. There are two easy ways around that—you can go with a classic that almost everyone likes, or you can give a discovery set and let them find a favorite on their own time. We’ve rounded up a short list of both, so whether they’ve been wearing the same scent since college or still haven’t found their signature, there’s something here that’ll end up in their perfume collection.

If you’re shopping for someone who already loves Coco Mademoiselle, this set is a no-brainer. It pairs the full 3.4-ounce bottle with the Twist and Spray travel size, so there’s one for their vanity and one for their bag, all in limited-edition holiday packaging. The scent opens with bright orange, softens into jasmine and May rose, and settles into patchouli and vetiver. It’s easy to see why it’s become one of Chanel’s most recognizable fragrances.

For someone who loves fragrance but hasn’t found their signature yet, this set from Hermès makes the search a lot more fun. It includes minis of four of the house’s best-known scents: the warm, spicy Eau des Merveilles, the ginger-and-tuberose Twilly d’Hermès, the green, mango-tinged Un Jardin sur le Nil, and the luminous floral Jour d’Hermès.

If someone on your list loves a perfume that makes them stand out, put this one at the top. Merit’s New Wave is an extrait, made with nearly 30 percent fragrance oil, so it lasts a lot longer than most eaux de parfum. It starts out a little spicy from pink pepper and gets warmer and sweeter as it wears, with orange blossom and honey up front and vanilla and incense underneath.

Not sure whether they’d like something light or something a little more intense? This set lets them try both. It comes with four minis of Cartier’s La Panthère, an eau de toilette, two eaux de parfum, and the parfum, and they all share the same mix of gardenia and soft musk. The eau de toilette is the lightest of the bunch and works for daytime, while the parfum is deeper and better for a night out.

Some of the best gifts aren’t about what goes on your face but about how you feel day-to-day. Wellness picks make sense for the person who’s always trying to sleep better, drink more water, or finally figure out why they wake up tired, and they tend to get used every single day. These four are easy upgrades that will fit right into your giftee’s routine, whether they’re a total wellness devotee or just curious.

Most people filter their drinking water without thinking twice, but the water they shower in every day rarely gets the same attention. Jolie’s shower head swaps in for your regular one and filters out chlorine and heavy metals, which can leave hair dry and dull and skin feeling tight after a shower. Over time, they should notice softer hair and clear, glowing skin becoming the norm.

Oura’s new Ring 5 is about 40% smaller than the last one and made from lightweight titanium, so it’s easy to forget it’s on—perfect for the person who has been complaining about their sleep for years. Each morning, the app shows how well they slept, how stressed their body was, and how they’re recovering. The battery lasts up to nine days, and the charging case holds about a month of backup power, so there’s no need to pack a charger for a long weekend away.

If anyone you know is obsessed with their oral hygiene, getting them the Rolls-Royce of toothbrushes will keep you slated as the ultimate gift giver forever. Polish, prestige, and next-generation cleanliness make Philips’s latest in dental technology the ideal present for those who like to get five stars every time they visit the dentist.

For the person who needs a little bit of calm in their life and has getting bigger muscles on their resolution list, the vibration plate is the perfect contribution toward their 2027 health goals. This version from HexaPlate uses side-to-side oscillation to tamp down an active nervous system if you just want a little bit of relaxation or to challenge the body when doing squats, lunges, or push-ups.

La Mer is one of those brands people love but rarely buy for themselves, so this set is a smart way in. For under $100, you get four minis worth $250 in total: the brand’s lightweight Moisturizing Soft Cream; the Resurfacing Treatment, a gentle liquid exfoliator; the Renewal Oil; and The Concentrate, a serum made to calm stressed, irritated skin. Everything comes zipped inside a velveteen case, which works just as well for travel once the minis are gone.

This is a great gift for anyone who’s been eyeing red-light therapy but isn’t ready to spend hundreds on a mask. The set pairs True Botanicals’ Pure Radiance Supreme Eye Cream, made to firm and smooth the skin around the eyes, with a small red-light wand that you glide along the orbital bone after applying the cream. The wand shuts itself off after two minutes, so there’s no guessing how long to use it on each eye. Worth $215 in total, it’s another Nordstrom exclusive.

If you know someone who’s obsessed with anything vanilla-scented, this set from Summer Fridays will go straight into their bag. It includes the brand’s cult-favorite Lip Butter Balm in Vanilla in full size, plus travel sizes of the Body Butter Balm and the Sunlit Vanilla Eau de Parfum, which smells warm and a little like dessert. The perfume slides into an exclusive key-chain holder, so it can clip onto a purse or keys for touch-ups throughout the day.

Byredo’s Bal d’Afrique has a way of turning up on just about everyone’s vanity, and once you’ve smelled it, it’s easy to see why. If there’s a fellow fan in your life, this mini set lets you give them the whole ritual without the full-size price tag. It includes the fragrance, a body wash, and a body lotion, so the scent carries from the shower through the rest of the day, plus a tiny key chain filled with the perfume that clips right onto a bag for touch-ups on the go.

When winter hits, body care quickly becomes one of the most practical gifts you can give. Between the cold air outside and the heaters running inside, skin tends to feel tight and dry by mid-December, and most people don’t realize how much they need a good body oil or scrub until one is in their hands. These sets cover every step, from a scrub that buffs away dry patches to a rich cream afterward, and a few come with scents nice enough that they double as fragrance. They’re also an easy pick when you’re not sure what someone’s skin type is, since nearly everyone could use a little extra moisture this time of year.

For the friend who reads ingredient lists and actually wants to see results, Osea’s holiday set is a smart pick. It starts with the brand’s body scrub, which buffs away dry, dull skin and leaves it glowing, followed by its algae-infused body oil to lock in moisture and help skin look firmer and more elastic over time. And the dry brush, for daily lymphatic drainage and sloughing away dead skin, will remain useful long after the body-care products run out.

Fit for the king or queen in your life, Flamingo Estate’s Jasmine Damask Rose Bathroom Set takes the bathroom experience to the next level. It includes hand wash, a scented candle, and a bar of soap that indulge the senses in the rich and luxurious fragrance note that David Lynch himself deemed “intoxicating.”

If there’s a Salt & Stone fan on your list, this three-piece set is an easy way to stock them up for less. It comes with the brand’s bestselling scent in three minis—a fragrance, a body wash, and a deodorant—so they can layer it from the shower through the end of the day. The body wash is made with nourishing botanicals that keep skin from feeling dry, and the deodorant lasts up to 24 hours, which makes the set as practical as it is nice to smell.

Soft Services’ bestselling hand cream was made for the nightstand, and now there’s a version for the desk too. The new Lumelo Weightless Hydrator is a great pick for your office bestie or the friend who’s always applying hand cream between meetings. Instead of the rich texture of the original, it has a light, gel-like feel that sinks in fast, so it’s easy to work into a midday break without leaving fingerprints on your laptop.

#6597. All About Bonnie-Chance Roberts, Beanie Feldstein’s Wife

Beanie Feldstein just shared a major life update: She and her wife, Bonnie-Chance Roberts, quietly welcomed their first child. “She is genuinely beyond my wildest dreams. I really did dream her,” Feldstein told People of their baby girl in November 2026.

In May, the actress announced her pregnancy on Instagram, writing, “Limited Edition Scouse Beanie Baby coming soon!! 🎀🍼.”

The announcement comes nearly two years after the couple married in a camp-themed celebration in upstate New York.

Feldstein often keeps the spotlight on her work, but when it comes to Roberts, she doesn’t hold back. Over the years, she’s shared glimpses into their relationship, from how they met on set to building a life together.

So who is Bonnie-Chance Roberts? Here’s everything to know about Feldstein’s wife and their life as parents.

Originally from Liverpool, Roberts works behind the scenes in the entertainment industry as a producer.

Her credits include projects like Mary Queen of Scots, Bridget Jones’s Baby, and How to Build a Girl—which she worked on as a producer while Feldstein starred in it.

Feldstein and Roberts first connected while working on How to Build a Girl. Feldstein told Vogue in June 2023 that they initially met over Skype during the casting process. “Bon had been developing Caitlin Moran’s book How to Build a Girl into a movie for over five years when they finally started the casting process for Caitlin’s fictional proxy, Johanna, a 16-year-old girl from Wolverhampton, England,” Feldstein said. “With a dash of luck and a push from the universe, they ended up being open to meeting a Jewish girl from Los Angeles.”

Their working relationship quickly shifted. As Feldstein recalled to Vogue, “From the moment we first kissed, we both knew we would get married and months after that, Bon had announced that when the time came, she wanted to be the one to propose to me.”

The relationship grew steadily from there. By 2020, Feldstein publicly celebrated Roberts on Instagram, writing in a birthday tribute, “I’m pretty convinced you’re actually made of magic. The girl with the warmest heart, the most expansive imagination, and the most exceptional brain. I love you so much. Happy birthday, bubba!!!”

The couple didn’t keep things private for long. In September 2019, they stepped out together at the Toronto International Film Festival for the premiere of How to Build a Girl, marking their first red carpet appearance as a couple.

Roberts later posted about the experience on Instagram, writing, “They say it takes a village to build a girl, and they are right!”

Roberts took the lead when it came time to propose. Feldstein announced their engagement in June 2022, sharing photos from the moment on Instagram and captioning them, “I do, Bon.”

Roberts later described designing the ring during a long period when the couple lived apart due to the pandemic. “The dream was for the ring to look as if a shard of magic was frozen in time,” she told Vogue in 2023.

The couple tied the knot on May 20, 2023, at Cedar Lakes Estate in New York’s Hudson Valley.

The theme felt personal. Feldstein told Vogue, “I grew up going to summer camp for 10 years, and my parents and both sets of my grandparents met at summer camp, so camp is a lineage of love through the generations of my family. Even though we met in London and fell in love on a film set, to get married at a camp was a truly beautiful emotional homecoming.”

Roberts wore a tailored bridal suit for the ceremony, while Feldstein opted for a vintage-inspired Gucci gown.

Looking back on the day, Feldstein shared on Late Night with Seth Meyers in February 2024, “[My wedding] went so swimmingly,” she said. “Like, I’m such an anxious girly. And I was more calm at the wedding than I am, like, brushing my teeth, at the supermarket. I was so calm. I just got to look at her and hear her vows, and it was perfect.”

“We wrote our own vows, and it actually rained a little the day of our wedding, and we handwrote the vows and the trees sort of shook and dripped on my vows,” she continued. “And I was like, ‘Oh, I hope I know them by heart.’ But it was fine. It was actually all going perfectly.”

In May 2026, Feldstein and Roberts announced they were expecting their first child.

The couple shared the news with a joint Instagram post featuring a series of photos, including one of a cake decorated with pink bows and the message “B+B are having a baby!”

The announcement marked a new chapter for the couple—and a years-long dream realized for Feldstein. In 2021, the actress told Bustle, “Sixteen years from now I hope to be living in New York City or London, married to my girlfriend, and have babies and puppies running around while we both make movies, shows, and plays that feel meaningful and exciting and profound.”

Feldstein quietly welcomed her and Roberts’s baby girl. In a November 4 interview with People, she opened up about parenthood for the first time. She did not share her child’s name or birth date but marveled about life with her.

“She is genuinely beyond my wildest dreams. I really did dream her,” Feldstein said. “I always wanted to be a mom, and I always wanted a daughter. I look at her every day, and I’m like, ‘You’re just beyond anything I could have even tried to imagine.’”

“I love getting to watch her take in the world; it’s just the greatest gift. And getting to be a mom alongside my wife is the greatest gift,” she added. “She’s such a good mom, and it’s so special to watch. Motherhood is unbelievably beautiful.”

She reflected on one milestone she saw a few weeks before her interview. “There’s nothing like the first smile,” she said. “I could feel her soul from the moment she was born. I remember people told me newborns are little blobs and they don’t really come alive until 6 weeks. I disagree with that completely. I could feel her soul from the moment I met her, but when you get to see that externalized in the smile, it’s so magic.”

Feldstein doesn’t shy away from expressing how much Roberts means to her.

Speaking to People in February 2024, she said of married life, “My favorite part of married life is everything, but I think the big thing that felt different was saying ‘my wife.’ [It] has more power than like ‘my girlfriend’…you know, it’s like ‘my wife’ is like ‘oh, this is legit.’”

She added, “Oh my god, I just want her with me every second of every day.”

In her November 2026 interview with People, she touched on her gratitude raising a child with Roberts. “I don’t think anyone that has had a baby can look at their child and not just feel the most gratitude to the universe,” Feldstein said. “I feel very grateful every day that I get to be her mom and mother alongside my wife and watch her with my whole family.”

#6596. Why Do We Keep Coming Back to Godzilla?

Like most people born in the western world after 1954, I knew of a monster named Godzilla before I’d heard of a country called Japan. It’s not a rare perspective. For as long as nearly any living person can remember, Godzilla has been hugely popular, far exceeding the global recognition afforded most leaders, athletes, and certainly his human co-stars, those men and women whose dramatic dealings are the universally agreed-upon bargain for apocalyptic havoc that millions upon millions have gladly paid to see for over 70 years.

What Godzilla hasn’t been is prestigious. The irradiated dinosaur of very few words—mainly deafening screams—is a beloved figure more in the key of Harry Potter, Batman, or James Bond than the loftier fare that typically gets recognized by major festivals or awards bodies. But exceptions to the rule do exist. The Criterion Collection issued Ishiro Honda's 1954 original on a deluxe Blu-ray in 2012 and marked their 1,000th release with a lavish set of Godzilla’s Shōwa era (1954-1975), which both documents film history and calls to mind John Huston’s Chinatown line about sticking around long enough to become respectable. Writing an introduction to Honda’s biography A Life in Film, from Godzilla to Kurosawa, Martin Scorsese deemed the series’ first director "an extraordinary artist and craftsman" and placed Honda’s 1954 film (alongside spin-offs Mothra and Rodan) among “pictures that haunted the imaginations of young moviegoers like myself and millions of others for years to come.” Kiyoshi Kurosawa—perhaps Japan’s greatest living filmmaker, and certainly its finest practitioner of austere horror—deemed Honda’s film an early lesson in national trauma. Thomas Pynchon, too, had ambitious plans to write a novel about the insurance adjuster who responds to Godzilla’s wreckage (the idea never fully materialized, though it did become a nice tangent in his 1990 novel Vineland). We can look at the films and countenance such appreciations from geniuses. In the meantime, good luck to anyone counting the exact number of action figures, coloring books, sticker packs, and lunchboxes boasting Godzilla and friends.

A critical shift started somewhere in the last decade. Toho ostensibly shelved Godzilla with 2004’s Final Wars, a grand finale that was the big-budget equivalent of a child smashing toys. (That is a compliment.) Godzilla LLC boasts enough films and ancillary products to be financially solvent until the sun burns out (or an indomitable monster rises from the sea), but that retirement was short-lived. Toho resurrected the franchise in aggressive form with 2016’s Shin Godzilla, both a complete series reboot and (across several stages, each grotesque and terrifying) character reinvention that dispensed with typical monster-movie hijinks. An unholy experiment that would make the series’ many mad scientists proud, Shin Godzilla fused the hilarious bureaucratic hallway-rushing of In the Loop or Veep with cosmic horror befitting its director, Hideaki Anno, whose contributions to Japanese culture are nearly Godzilla’s equal on the strength of Neon Genesis Evangelion alone. With time, it’s downright eerie to see Anno’s foreshadowing of the global unrest of Trump, Brexit, COVID, and our endless misinformation era. But rather than keep the great filmmaker on retainer for any number of sequels or spin-offs, Toho regrettably followed Shin Godzilla with an anime trilogy produced for Netflix, a rare class of films I’ve been too embarrassed to even log on Letterboxd.

Whether genius or dreck, none of these films quite anticipated 2023’s Godzilla Minus One. It’s one thing to become the highest-grossing Japanese-language release in U.S. history—any Godzilla movie that doesn't at least aim for such a distinction isn’t worth its salt. It’s harder to imagine anyone, even or especially the franchise’s most ardent fans, anticipated lavish public praise from a quintet of Best Director winners in Steven Spielberg (who claims to have seen the film at least three times), James Cameron (who offered to work on a sequel), Christopher Nolan, Guillermo Del Toro, and Bong Joon-ho. In a recorded conversation with Yamazaki, Tom Cruise and Christopher McQuarrie credited the film as an inspiration; the actor went so far as to call it “perfect.” Which is to say nothing of the fact that Godzilla Minus One earned the series its first Oscar, a VFX prize awarded to none other than writer-director Takashi Yamazaki—a nice encapsulation of the film’s balance between spirit and spectacle.

Because Godzilla Minus One resonated more than anyone could have anticipated, Godzilla Minus Zero, which arrives in theaters this weekend, shoulders the burden of expectation. The first shot across the bow was its world premiere at last month’s New York Film Festival, where Zero debuted alongside prestige fare like Luca Guadagnino’s Sam Altman biopic Artificial and Tony Gilroy’s star-studded Behemoth! There, NYFF’s artistic director Dennis Lim introduced the movie to a sold-out crowd at the Alice Tully Hall, praising Yamazaki for exemplifying "the endless possibilities of creative VFX and genre filmmaking." Minus Zero indeed thrives on spectacle: its opening sequence blazes a merciless path of carnage aided by an elegant long take, while subsequent scenes centered on one of Godzilla’s classic foes, the three-headed Ghidorah, inspire genuine terror more than cheap thrills. This is the first Japanese film shot for IMAX, a large-scale exhibition that’s often torqued for discomfort. Yamazaki’s centerpiece battle pitting the monster against a squadron of fighter planes is dogged by fatalistic doom: a mother and child screaming as their house crashes to the ground don’t get the last-minute salvation we’ve come to expect, and even the sentimental-seeming inclusion of a pilot named Honda is complicated by his eventual fate.

If not quite so grave as the visions of death that imprinted upon a young Kiyoshi Kurosawa, Yamazaki’s narrative—including a face-melting sequence that U.S. distributor GKIDS have asked not be spoiled—provides a stark contrast to the bloodless carnage of American blockbusters. It’s quite the cultural coup, too, that a film this brutal and generally skeptical of American imperialism has secured a simultaneous international release: every English-speaking actor (none recognizable, each portraying arrogant allied military) bears an amusingly off-market quality à la the nefarious white time-travelers of 1991’s altogether underrated Godzilla vs. King Ghidorah.

Nearly all Godzilla films are a total restart. Minus Zero is immediately notable as a direct sequel. The results suggest that Yamazaki overestimated his initial project. Godzilla is not much of a presence in Minus Zero, first appearing around the 50-minute mark and then again in a suitable, albeit brief climax. Far more time is spent with those we came to know and like during Minus One, each reprised by an entirely competent ensemble that fails to elevate interest higher than a certain co-star’s 50 meters. (The protagonists’ adopted daughter from Minus One returns here for the sole purpose of standing in place and crying.) Whatever its pretensions towards grandeur, this is still a film where a scientist explains his master plan by smashing together two monster figures. It takes little to delight in this moment, a literal and figurative collision of serious storytelling and childlike abandon. More of that spirit might’ve served the final picture.

My mild disappointment is nothing compared to the agony Godzilla has wreaked on the district of Ginza, which last week hosted the first public screenings of Minus Zero through the Tokyo International Film Festival. Godzilla’s annihilated the city’s landmarks enough times that when we think of all-out destruction on the sprawling megalopolis that is Tokyo, we’re probably picturing its uber-fashionable shopping sector laid to ruins. When he emerged from the sea in 1954, he wrecked the district’s historic Nichigeki Theater, which was again destroyed (in real life, of humans’ accord) and reopened as the Yurakucho Mullion building in 1984—the same year as The Return of Godzilla, where he inflicted yet more damage on the brand-new structure. Godzilla Minus One recreated the Nichigeki Theater in loving detail only to destroy it again in a sequence that deployed modern visual effects to cause maximum tactility and human misery. That Hiroshima-like site is revisited in Minus Zero, leading one character to declare that “Ginza is again the battleground.” Time’s healed those wounds, however. The night before Minus Zero’s Japanese premiere, a small crowd gathered outside the Yurakucho Mullion’s Seiko watch for an extravagant display: the clock lifted, and out came a small set of Godzilla puppets that strike chimes while Akira Ifukube’s iconic theme plays.

Ginza’s Wako Clock Tower has fared no better: it was torn to ribbons in the 1954 original, 1995’s Godzilla vs. Destoroyah, Shin Godzilla, and Minus One. After a time you must wonder what keeps bringing Godzilla back to the neighborhood. Is it animal instinct, or mere coincidence, or an atomic hatred for its glowing consumerism? The Wako Annex, a nearby pastry shop that Google not-inaccurately describes as “chic,” currently advertises a Christmas-themed cake recreation of the oft-doomed Clock Tower with Minus Zero’s monster looming over it; accompanying text informs us that “Godzilla strikes Ginza’s Wako once again.” The nearby Toho cinema is within Hibiya Godzilla Square, featuring a small but impressively detailed statue and a plaque reading, “The human race must coexist with Godzilla.” Immediately adjacent is a three-story shopping mall hosting a Toho store selling numerous Godzilla ephemera. (I bought the tea cup.)

Even Americans accustomed to the fetishization of disaster would be impressed by Japan’s ability to marry suffering and spectacle to great financial gain. Perhaps it’s the same haunted fascination of a young Martin Scorsese or Kiyoshi Kurosawa cast unto the world at large; Godzilla might be scary as he destroys Ginza, but he’s something to admire when shrunk down to human size and displayed inside the Yurakucho Mullion’s lobby. (The photo-snapping crowds that gather every time I walk past suggest that bit of marketing paid off.) Even as Minus Zero’s first reviews show a less rapturous response than Minus One, this series’ viability—and its newfound prestige—shows little indication of flagging. Ginza’s residents were beyond happy to see Godzilla, at least in ossified, action-figure form. But who's to say they wouldn't be just as excited if, one day, his path of destruction broke through the screen?
